Thermal Hall response of an abelian chiral spin liquid at finite temperatures

Avijit Maity Affiliation: Department of Theoretical Physics, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Homi Bhabha Road, Colaba, Mumbai 400005, India.    Haoyu Guo Affiliation: Laboratory of Atomic and Solid State Physics, Cornell University,
142 Sciences Drive, Ithaca, New York 14853-2501, USA    Subir Sachdev Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, USA    Vikram Tripathi Affiliation: Department of Theoretical Physics, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Homi Bhabha Road, Colaba, Mumbai 400005, India.
Abstract

Thermal Hall transport has emerged as a valuable tool for probing the fractionalized excitations in chiral quantum spin liquids. Observing quantized thermal Hall response, expected at temperatures below the spectral gap, has been challenging and controversial. The finite temperature behavior, especially in the quantum critical regime above the spectral gap, can provide useful signatures of the underlying topological order. In this context, we study the spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a kagome lattice that is believed to be a U(1)(1) Dirac spin liquid over a wide intermediate energy range. Scalar spin chirality perturbations turn this into a gapped abelian chiral spin liquid (CSL) with semionic topological order. Using a recently developed large-NN technique [Guo et al., Phys. Rev. B 101, 195126 (2020)], we obtain explicit expressions for the thermal Hall conductivity κx​y\kappa_{xy} at finite temperatures taking into account both matter and gauge fluctuations. At low temperatures below the spectral gap, the quantized thermal Hall response agrees with that expected from conformal field theory and gravitational anomaly arguments. Our main finding is that in a large temperature window spanning the spectral gap and the Curie temperature scales where quantum critical fluctuations dominate, κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T obeys a power-law with logarithmic corrections. Our analysis also provides a route to understanding the thermal Hall response at higher temperatures in the quantum critical regime.

I Introduction

Following Anderson’s introduction of the resonating valence bond (RVB) state concept [1], substantial progress has been made in unraveling the mysteries of quantum spin liquids (QSLs), an unconventional category of quantum phases that go beyond the traditional Landau symmetry-breaking framework [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. These states not only hold conceptual importance and relevance in experimental contexts but also intertwine with intricate issues, spanning topological order, strongly coupled gauge theories, and high-temperature superconductivity. These highly entangled quantum states are defined by charge-neutral spinons-excitations which are coupled with emergent gauge fields and carry fractional values of the integer spin.

The interest in chiral spin liquid (CSL), a subclass of QSLs that break time-reversal and parity symmetries, originated from the contributions of Kalmeyer and Laughlin [7, 8]. They suggested that frustrated magnets could host bosonic analogs of fractional quantum Hall states, giving rise to anyonic quasiparticles in the bulk and chiral gapless modes on the edge. These edge modes are described by (1+1)(1+1)-dimensional conformal field theories (CFT).

Thermal transport measurements offer an attractive means to probe the nature of spin liquid states as heat currents in insulating quantum magnets at low temperatures can get significant contributions from emergent and charge-neutral modes [9]. In this context, the thermal Hall effect is sensitive to the nature of elementary excitations (e.g. fermions or bosons) as well as the topological properties associated with their respective energy bands, in particular the Berry curvature of elementary excitations [10, 11]. For example, thermal Hall measurements have been used to reveal intrinsic topological properties of quantum Hall liquids such as the non-Abelian nature of the ν=5/2\nu=5/2 fractional quantum Hall liquid [12].

The distinctive feature expected from the abelian CSL state is the quantization of thermal Hall conductivity in the zero temperature limit in units of (π​kB2/6​ℏ)​T(\pi k_{B}^{2}/6\hbar)\,T. This quantization arises from the chiral central charge of the chiral edge theory, which is an integer for abelian CSLs [13, 14, 15]. In contrast, for non-abelian CSLs, the chiral central charge can have a more complex expression [16, 17]. The Kitaev model is an exactly solvable model with exact spin liquid ground-state [18]; under the influence of a magnetic field, this model exhibits a gapped phase characterized by topological order, accommodating non-Abelian Ising anyons [19]. The presence of a chiral Majorana fermion edge state suggests an anticipated response of half-quantized thermal Hall conductivity at T→0T\rightarrow 0. Such a conductivity has been claimed to be observed in α\alpha-RuCl3 [20], but this remains controversial [21, 22, 23]. Another recent discovery of an enhanced thermal Hall conductivity in cuprates [24, 25] has sparked considerable interest in unraveling its underlying mechanism: this was initially proposed to be associated with topological spin excitations [26, 27], but now appears more likely to be associated with phonons [28, 29].

Detecting a quantized thermal Hall effect, expected theoretically at low temperatures, has been both technically challenging and widely debated in experiments. At higher temperatures, especially in the quantum critical regime above the spectral gap, the thermal Hall response shows different behavior, creating a chance to observe topological order in ways that don’t appear as clearly at lower temperatures. At these low temperatures, thermal Hall conductivity in topological phases is linked to chiral edge states and gravitational anomaly, which connects edge and bulk properties. However, this interpretation doesn’t apply at finite temperatures above 2+1-dimensional quantum critical points. In this work, we examine the thermal Hall effect of fermionic matter interacting with emergent gauge fields, representing a low-energy effective theory for the CSL phase stabilized on a kagome lattice.

Quantum Heisenberg antiferromagnets on two-dimensional kagome lattices offer an ideal platform for investigating exotic spin liquid states and have been used to model materials like Volborthite and Herbertsmithite [30, 31]. Understanding the ground state of the antiferromagnetic spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg model on a kagome lattice remains a highly challenging problem in quantum magnetism. Numerous theoretical proposals have been suggested, with the most promising contenders currently being the gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid [32, 33, 34] and the gapless U(1)(1) Dirac spin liquid (DSL) [35]. Initial investigations using density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) techniques indicated the presence of a gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid [36, 37, 38]. More recent work supports U(1)(1) DSL over a significant energy range. Notably, variational Monte Carlo [39, 40, 41, 42, 43], more recent DMRG [44, 45], and two-dimensional tensor network studies [46, 47] are consistent with a DSL, but an eventual transition at the lowest energies to a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid with a small gap is not ruled out [48, 49, 50]. Direct experimental observation and characterization of QSLs remain challenging. However, their fractionalized excitations can be probed using conventional techniques. For instance, in the specific case of the U(1)(1) DSL on the spin-1/21/2 kagome lattice, Raman spectroscopy has been proposed as a tool to detect the spinon continuum as well as fluctuations of the emergent gauge field [51].

In kagome antiferromagnets, a CSL was stabilized by the addition of scalar chirality terms to the Hamiltonian [52] that explicitly breaks parity and time-reversal symmetry but not spin rotation symmetry. Utilizing DMRG, the authors of Ref. [52] demonstrated that, particularly under a strong enough time-reversal symmetry breaking term, the ground state is a CSL state, sharing the same topological class (semionic topological order) as the ν=1/2\nu=1/2 Laughlin state. It is also known [53] that such CSL states can appear as a result of spontaneous symmetry breaking in kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnets with further-neighbor interactions. CSLs also have been discovered in diverse theoretical studies for different models in more recent investigations [54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61].

The thermal Hall response has been observed in the spin-liquid phase of kagome antiferromagnets, such as volborthite [62] and Cakapellasite (Ca-K) [63, 64]. Previous studies have extensively explored the theoretical aspects of the thermal Hall effect in insulating phases on kagome lattices [10, 65, 66, 67]. For example, in weak Mott insulating U(1)(1) spin liquids with spinon Fermi surface, it has been shown that external magnetic fields induce internal U(1)(1) gauge flux, impacting neutral spinons and contributing to the thermal Hall effect [10]. The thermal Hall effect in the strong Mott regime of QSL originates from the effective generation of an internal U(1)(1) gauge flux for spinons induced by an external magnetic field through the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, as demonstrated in Ref. [67].

In this paper, we analyze the thermal Hall response of the Heisenberg spin model on the kagome lattice, offering an effective description of the low-energy characteristics of the Hubbard model, when subjected to a time-reversal symmetry-breaking term. The spin liquid state on the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet model, found to be close to a chiral spin liquid stabilized by longer-ranged spin exchange interactions [54, 53], suggests a potential continuous transition [55]; this transition is easily understood when considering the ground state of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the kagome lattice as a gapless U(1)(1) DSL. In this study, rather than directly addressing a specific numerical solution for a spin model on the kagome lattice, we assume the system stabilizes a gapless U(1)(1) DSL and illustrate the emergence of quantized thermal Hall conductivity with the introduction of a time-reversal symmetry-breaking term. The key new ingredient distinguishing our approach from earlier mean-field studies of the kagome antiferromagnets based on partons or spin waves is that we take into account the effect of gauge fluctuations following Guo et al. [17], and show that it changes the quantized value of the low-temperature thermal Hall response and also strongly affects the finite temperature behavior.

We now describe our main findings. Our analysis is consistent with semionic topological order in the CSL phase. The (chiral) central charge inferred from the U(1)(1) Dirac Chern-Simons theory has the value c−=1c_{-}=1 consistent with recent DMRG-based numerical analysis [52]. On the other hand, neglecting gauge contributions would have given us (erroneously) a chiral central charge of c−=2c_{-}=2 based on purely mean field parton theory. The peculiar distribution of the Chern numbers of the occupied parton bands results in non-monotonic temperature dependence of the free parton thermal Hall response, reminiscent of the observed experimental behavior in some of the kagome antiferromagnet systems [62, 63, 64]. For finite temperature properties that account for the gauge fluctuation effects, we take a large-NfN_{f} linear response approach. The leading order gauge fluctuation effects in the thermal Hall response are governed by Aslamazov-Larkin type processes [17] which are 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) in the large-NfN_{f} expansion. Remarkably, higher order corrections vanish in the zero temperature limit, which means the contribution of gauge fluctuations to the chiral central charge is independent of NfN_{f} in contrast with the non-abelian counterpart [17]. At finite temperatures, it is crucial to consider the effects of matter and gauge excitations along with their interactions. We present explicit expressions for the finite-temperature thermal Hall response, specifically computing the Aslamazov-Larkin diagram at finite temperature while using a temperature-dependent Maxwell-Chern-Simons action for the gauge field, where we observe a logarithmic behavior at very high temperatures. More generally, our approach should be relevant for arbitrary abelian chiral spin liquids.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We begin in Sec. II by setting up the mean-field formalism for the CSL state on the kagome lattice using the Abrikosov fermion (parton). Here we discuss the continuum limit of the mean-field state and the effect of gauge fluctuation. Sec. IV evaluates the thermal Hall effect in the CSL state. We describe the thermal Hall response of the U(1)(1) Dirac Chern-Simons theory in the 1/Nf1/N_{f} expansion in Sec. V.

II The model and spin fractionalization

Consider a spin S=1/2S=1/2 antiferromagnet on the kagome lattice described by the Hamiltonian

H=H1+Hχ,H=H_{1}+H_{\chi}, (1)

where

H1\displaystyle H_{1} =\displaystyle= J1​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩𝑺𝒊⋅𝑺𝒋,\displaystyle J_{1}\sum_{\langle\bm{ij}\rangle}\bm{S}_{\bm{i}}\cdot\bm{S}_{\bm{j}}, (2)
Hχ\displaystyle H_{\chi} =\displaystyle= Jχ​∑𝒊​𝒋​𝒌∈Δ,∇𝑺𝒊⋅(𝑺𝒋×𝑺𝒌),\displaystyle J_{\chi}\sum_{\bm{ijk}\in\Delta,\nabla}\bm{S}_{\bm{i}}\cdot(\bm{S}_{\bm{j}}\times\bm{S}_{\bm{k}}), (3)

𝑺𝒊\bm{S}_{\bm{i}} are the spin-1/21/2 degrees of freedome on the sites 𝒊.\bm{i}. H1H_{1} describes nearest-neighbor Heisenberg interaction which preserves the global SU(2)(2) rotation in spin space, time-reversal, and all the discrete lattice symmetries on the kagome lattice. HχH_{\chi} describes scalar spin chirality interaction on the elementary triangles, which breaks time-reversal symmetry and parity but preserves global SU(2)(2) spin rotation symmetry. JχJ_{\chi} can originate, for example, in the presence of an external magnetic field: in this case, its magnitude is directly proportional to the sine of the magnetic flux through each elementary triangle of the kagome lattice [68]. An external magnetic field also generates a Zeeman coupling which will break the spin rotational symmetry and degeneracy. For small external fields that do not cause phase transitions in the model of Eq. (1), we may safely disregard this term in the rest of the analysis.

II.1 Parton mean-field theory

To characterize the spin liquid state, we utilize a parton construction wherein we decompose the spin operator into spin-1/21/2 charge-neutral fermionic spinons f𝒊​αf_{\bm{i}\alpha}, (α=↑,↓\alpha=\uparrow,\downarrow), commonly referred to as Abrikosov fermions:

𝑺𝒊=12​f𝒊​α†​𝝈α​β​f𝒊​β,{\bm{S}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{i}}=\frac{1}{2}\,f_{\bm{i}\alpha}^{\dagger}{\bm{\sigma}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha\beta}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{i}\beta}, (4)

where 𝝈\bm{\sigma} denotes the Pauli matrices. The transformation from the spin-1/21/2 Hilbert space to the fermionic counterpart involves an expansion of the Hilbert space. To remain within the physical Hilbert space, we have to impose the following local single-site occupancy constraint, f𝒊​α†​f𝒊​α=1f_{\bm{i}\alpha}^{\dagger}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{i}\alpha}=1, where the summation over repeating indices is implied. Consequently, the fermionic band structure of spinons is consistently constrained to operate at half-filling. Furthermore, Eq. (4) has an SU(2)(2) gauge redundancy because of particle-hole symmetry in the fermion representation. When applying mean-field decoupling to handle spin interactions, it becomes necessary to incorporate a SU(2)(2) gauge field defined on the lattice links. The nature of the saddle points in the mean-field theory determines whether they lead to a breakdown of SU(2)(2) symmetry into either U(1)(1) or ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, depending on their specific structural characteristics [3, 69].

In the case where Jχ=0J_{\chi}=0, we consider the ground state of the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet as the U(1)(1) DSL. We initiate our analysis from the U(1)(1) DSL ansatz on the kagome lattice, commonly referred to as the ‘π\pi-flux’ state [35, 39]. Employing the conventional parton mean-field decoupling in the particle-hole channel for the Heisenberg interactions as described in Eq. (2) [3], we derive

H1,MF=−J12∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩,α[(f𝒊​α†f𝒋​αχ𝒋​𝒊+H.c.)−|χ𝒋​𝒊|2],H_{1,\text{MF}}=-\frac{J_{1}}{2}\sum_{\langle\bm{i}\bm{j}\rangle,\alpha}\left[(f^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{j}\alpha}\,\chi_{\bm{ji}}+\text{H.c.})-\lvert\chi_{\bm{ji}}\rvert^{2}\right], (5)

where χ𝒊​𝒋=∑α⟨f𝒊​α†​f𝒋​α⟩=χ𝒋​𝒊∗\chi_{\bm{ij}}^{\phantom{*}}=\sum_{\alpha}\langle f^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{j}\alpha}\rangle=\chi_{\bm{ji}}^{*}. In the case of the kagome lattice, these mean-field states are identified by the fluxes passing through the triangles and hexagons. Realizing the U(1)(1) DSL on the kagome lattice involves considering the hopping pattern depicted in Fig. 1, featuring zero flux through the triangular plaquettes and π\pi flux through the kagome hexagons [35, 39]. It is important to observe that the adoption of a six-site unit cell is intended to accommodate the underlying π\pi-flux per hexagon. The π\pi-flux ansatz leads to a magnetic Brillouin zone that is halved as shown in the Fig. 2a, featuring two Dirac cones at momenta ±𝑸\pm\bm{Q}, where 𝑸=(0,π/3)\bm{Q}=(0,\pi/\sqrt{3}), for each spinon species as shown in Fig. 2b.

Next, we discuss the impact of a scalar spin chirality term on the U(1)(1) DSL ansatz defined on the kagome lattice. Using the parton representation in Eq. (4), we decouple the three spin interaction in Eq. (3) into fermion bilinears by utilizing the same mean-field parameters (see Appendix A),

Hχ,MF=\displaystyle H_{\chi,\text{MF}}={} 3​i​Jχ16​∑𝒊​𝒋​𝒌,α(χ𝒊​𝒌​χ𝒌​𝒋​f𝒋​α†​f𝒊​α+χ𝒊​𝒌​χ𝒋​𝒊​f𝒌​α†​f𝒋​αCLOSE\displaystyle\frac{3iJ_{\chi}}{16}\sum_{\bm{ijk},\alpha}\Big(\chi_{\bm{ik}}\chi_{\bm{kj}}f^{\dagger}_{\bm{j}\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{i}\alpha}+\chi_{\bm{ik}}\chi_{\bm{ji}}f^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{j}\alpha}
OPEN+χ𝒌​𝒋​χ𝒋​𝒊​f𝒊​α†​f𝒌​α−χ𝒊​𝒌​χ𝒌​𝒋​χ𝒋​𝒊−H.c.).\displaystyle+\chi_{\bm{kj}}\chi_{\bm{ji}}f^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{k}\alpha}-\chi_{\bm{ik}}\chi_{\bm{kj}}\chi_{\bm{ji}}-\text{H.c.}\Big). (6)

Adding (5) and (6), the full mean-field spin Hamiltonian can be written as HMF=H1,MF+Hχ,MFH_{\text{MF}}=H_{1,\text{MF}}+H_{\chi,\text{MF}}. Without going into the self-consistent mean-field analysis, for the sake of generality, we opt to treat χ𝒊​𝒋\chi_{\bm{ij}} as free (bounded) parameters and assume χ𝒊​𝒋=|χ𝒊​𝒋|​ei​ϕ𝒊​𝒋\chi_{\bm{ij}}=\absolutevalue{\chi_{\bm{ij}}}e^{i\phi_{\bm{ij}}}, where |χ𝒊​𝒋|=χ\absolutevalue{\chi_{\bm{ij}}}=\chi is the amplitude and ϕ𝒊​𝒋\phi_{\bm{ij}} are the bond-dependent phases. Observing that χ𝒊​𝒋∗=χ𝒋​𝒊\chi^{*}_{\bm{ij}}=\chi^{\phantom{*}}_{\bm{ji}}, it implies that χ𝒊​𝒋\chi^{\phantom{*}}_{\bm{ij}} is a directed field, requiring an orientation choice for each link. When moving from 𝒊\bm{i} to 𝒋\bm{j}, χ𝒊​𝒋\chi^{\phantom{*}}_{\bm{ij}} is considered in the direction indicated by the arrow, and χ𝒊​𝒋∗\chi^{*}_{\bm{ij}} is taken opposite to the direction of the arrow, as depicted in Fig. 1. Now we can express the full mean-field spin Hamiltonian as follows

HMF=−t∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩,αei​θ𝒊​𝒋f†𝒊​αf𝒋​α+H.c.,H_{\rm{MF}}=-t\sum_{\langle\bm{ij}\rangle,\alpha}e^{i\theta_{\bm{ij}}}f^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{j}\alpha}+\text{H.c.}, (7)

where tt and θ𝒊​𝒋\theta_{\bm{ij}} can be computed from the values of J1J_{1}, JχJ_{\chi}, χ\chi and ϕ𝒊​𝒋\phi_{\bm{ij}} (see Appendix A).

Now total flux enclosed within a single triangular plaquette is given by θ𝒊​𝒋+θ𝒋​𝒌+θ𝒌​𝒊=ϕ\theta_{\bm{ij}}+\theta_{\bm{jk}}+\theta_{\bm{ki}}=\phi. We start from the U(1)(1) DSL, and CSL state emerges when an additional phase, represented by θ\theta, is incorporated into the directed links on the kagome lattice. Here, we consider a configuration where the up and down triangles share the same fluxes (i.e., ϕ=3​θ\phi=3\theta), and the hexagon’s flux is π−6​θ\pi-6\theta. This configuration can be denoted as [ϕ,π−2​ϕ]=[3​θ,π−6​θ]\left[\phi,\pi-2\phi\right]=\left[3\theta,\pi-6\theta\right], as discussed in Refs. [39, 56]. To achieve this, a magnetic unit cell with six sites is required, deviating from the standard three-site unit cell commonly used for the kagome lattice, as also employed for the U(1)(1) DSL.

Following the procedure in Appendix A, we diagonalize the Hamiltonian in Eq. (7) for the flux configuration [ϕ,π−2​ϕ]\left[\phi,\pi-2\phi\right]. When ϕ\phi is set to zero, the ansatz simplifies to the well-known U(1)(1) DSL state, resulting in a spectrum featuring a pair of Dirac cones centered at half-filling for each spinon species, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. So time-reversal symmetry is preserved for ϕ=0\phi=0. Moving forward, we examine flux phases characterized by a non-zero flux within triangles. The flux configuration [ϕ,π−2​ϕ]\left[\phi,\pi-2\phi\right] with ϕ≠0\phi\neq 0 breaks both time-reversal and parity symmetry while maintaining the combined symmetry of the two. The introduction of any nonzero value for ϕ\phi leads to the emergence of a direct gap at each Dirac cone as shown in Fig. 2c. The lower three bands become fully occupied, while the upper three bands remain empty, maintaining the half-filling condition. We find that the filled bands have non-zero Chern numbers with values of C={−1,−1,1}C=\{-1,-1,1\} starting from the topmost occupied band, while the empty bands have corresponding Chern numbers of opposite sign. Taking into account the spin degeneracy, the net Chern number of the occupied bands amounts to −2-2, corresponding to a CSL phase. Consequently, the resulting fully gapped bands exhibit topologically nontrivial characteristics.

II.2 The continuum field theory and gauge fluctuation

Having obtained a mean-field description of the U(1)(1) DSL and CSL phases, we now derive the continuum low-energy effective field theory and consider the effect of gauge fluctuations.

Here we briefly discuss the effective theory of the U(1)(1) DSL on the kagome lattice. Given the π\pi-flux ansatz on the kagome lattice, featuring gapless Dirac cones at the Fermi level, our focus is narrowed to the two bands that intersect the Fermi level. Consequently, in the continuum limit, we can characterize the low-energy spinons near the Dirac points using the relativistic Lagrangian for massless Dirac fermions [39, 70],

ℒ1,MF=ψ¯l(iγμ∂μ)ψl,{\cal L}_{{1,\rm MF}}=\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\left(i\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\right)\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}, (8)

where ψl\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l} is a two-component spinor whose flavor index ll is summed from 11 to NfN_{f}. The gamma matrices are taken to be γμ=(τz,i​τy,−i​τx)\gamma^{\mu}=(\tau^{z},i\tau^{y},-i\tau^{x}), where the τa\tau^{a}’s are Pauli matrices acting on spinor (sublattice) indices and ψ¯l≡ψl†​τz\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\equiv\psi^{\dagger}_{l}\tau^{z}. The dispersion of the U(1)(1) DSL on the kagome lattice features two Dirac cones, resulting in a total of Nf=4N_{f}=4 when accounting for spin.

In characterizing the phase fluctuation of the mean-field ansatz, we represent χ𝒊​𝒋\chi_{\bm{ij}} as χ𝒊​𝒋=χ¯𝒊​𝒋​e−i​a𝒊​𝒋\chi_{\bm{ij}}=\bar{\chi}_{\bm{ij}}e^{-ia_{\bm{ij}}}. Including the phase fluctuation, the mean-field Hamiltonian in Eq. (5) becomes

H1,U⁡(1)=−J12∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩,α(χ¯𝒋​𝒊e−i​a𝒋​𝒊f𝒊​α†f𝒋​α+H.c.).H_{1,\mathrm{U}(1)}=-\frac{J_{1}}{2}\sum_{\langle\bm{i}\bm{j}\rangle,\alpha}\left(\bar{\chi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{ji}}\,e^{-ia_{\bm{ji}}}\,f^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{j}\alpha}+\text{H.c.}\right). (9)

The Hamiltonian in Eq. (9) is invariant under the gauge transformation

f𝒊→f𝒊​ei​θ𝒊,a𝒊​𝒋→a𝒊​𝒋+θ𝒊−θ𝒋.f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{i}}\rightarrow f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{i}}e^{i\theta_{\bm{i}}},\qquad a_{\bm{ij}}\rightarrow a_{\bm{ij}}+\theta_{\bm{i}}-\theta_{\bm{j}}. (10)

In this context, a𝒊​𝒋a_{\bm{ij}} serves as the spatial component of U(1)(1) gauge field. The single-particle occupancy constraint can be enforced by including a Lagrange multiplier a0​(𝒊,t)a_{0}(\bm{i},t), which corresponds to the time component of the gauge field aμa_{\mu}. Namely, we have transformed the quantum spin model into a scenario where spinons are strongly coupled to the dynamical U(1)(1) gauge field.

Including minimal coupling of the U(1)(1) gauge field to the massless Dirac fermions, the Lagrangian in Eq. (8) becomes [39, 70],

ℒ1=ψ¯liγμ(∂μ−iaμ)ψl.{\cal L}_{1}=\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}i\gamma^{\mu}\big(\partial_{\mu}-ia_{\mu}\big)\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}. (11)

As explained in Sec. II.1, the addition of an extra phase θ\theta to the U(1)(1) DSL ansatz results in the opening of a direct gap at each Dirac cone. Consequently, this modification yields a CSL with a net Chern number of −2-2. For ϕ≠0\phi\neq 0, the Dirac fermions acquire “mass” (a “gap”) by breaking time-reversal symmetry. So in the DSL perspective, obtaining CSL involves introducing a mass term, ψ¯α​ψα\bar{\psi}_{\alpha}\psi_{\alpha}, with the same sign for all Nf=4N_{f}=4 Dirac cones. This leads to us to a continuum low-energy effective theory of the CSL phase which involves four species of Dirac fermions with mass mm interacting with the U(1)(1) gauge field aμa_{\mu}. However, we must not overlook the contribution of the two occupied “heavy” fermionic bands located significantly away from the Fermi level. These bands exhibit a non-zero Chern number, specifically C={−1,−1}C=\{-1,-1\} per spin species. Integrating out the heavy fermions generates a Chern-Simons term for the U(1) gauge field aμa_{\mu} with level 𝚔=−4\mathtt{k}=-4, accounting for spin degeneracy. In this manner, we obtain the Lagrangian of the U(1)(1) Dirac Chern-Simons theory in Minkowski space-time

ℒψ,a=ψ¯liγμ(∂μ−iaμ)ψl−mψ¯lψl+𝚔CS[aμ],{\cal L}_{\psi,a}=\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}i\gamma^{\mu}\big(\partial_{\mu}-ia_{\mu}\big)\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}-m\ \bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}+\mathtt{k}\ \text{CS}[a_{\mu}]\text{,} (12)

where the last term represents the U(1)(1) Chern-Simons term with level 𝚔=−4\mathtt{k}=-4. In the presence of a finite mass term mm, a gap forms, and each light Dirac fermion induces a Chern-Simons response proportional to sgn⁡(m)/2{\rm{sgn}}(m)/2. Upon integrating out the light fermions also, we obtain a U(1)𝚔^(1)_{\hat{\mathtt{k}}} Chern-Simons theory,

ℒa=𝚔^4​π​ϵμ​ν​ρ​aμ​∂νaρ,\mathcal{L}_{a}=\frac{\hat{\mathtt{k}}}{4\pi}\,\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho}\,a_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}a_{\rho}, (13)

where the integer 𝚔^\hat{\mathtt{k}} is defined by

𝚔^=𝚔+Nf2​sgn​(m).\hat{\mathtt{k}}=\mathtt{k}+\frac{N_{f}}{2}\,{\rm{sgn}}(m). (14)

As the Chern number of the band just below the Fermi level is C=+1C=+1, the sign of the mass term of the light Dirac fermion is positive i.e., m>0m>0, and we get a U(1)−2(1)_{-2} Chern-Simons theory, which is the effective field theory of the ν=1/2\nu=1/2 bosonic Laughlin state [8, 71]. So, the low energy physics of the CSL is captured by the following Lagrangian:

ℒa=−24​πϵμ​ν​ρaμ∂νaρ.\mathcal{L}_{a}=-\frac{2}{4\pi}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho}a_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}a_{\rho}. (15)

The Chern-Simons term induces a gap in the gauge particles, allowing us to ignore their fluctuations and the instanton effect in the low-energy description. So, the U(1)(1) gauge field can only help the spinons interact over short distances, making these fractionalized particles (spinons) the basic building blocks of the spin liquid ground state. Hence, the chiral gapped spin liquid remains robust against gauge fluctuations and retains its physical significance.

We highlight certain characteristics of the CSL state governed by the effective theory in Eq. (15). It shows a twofold degeneracy in its ground state on a torus. The Chern-Simons term induces a change in the spinons’ statistics, transforming them into “semions” with a statistical angle of π/2\pi/2 and a fractional charge of 1/21/2. The two abelian anyons (trivial and semion) imply a total quantum dimension 𝒟=2,\mathcal{D}=\sqrt{2}, and a nontrivial topological entanglement entropy γ=ln⁡𝒟=12​ln⁡2.\gamma=\ln\mathcal{D}=\frac{1}{2}\ln 2. In a system with an open boundary, the CSL state has a chiral edge state characterized by the U(1)(1) Kac-Moody theory at level 22. Therefore, the chiral state that emerges is consistent with the one previously identified by Bauer and co-workers in Ref. [52].

III Edge and bulk perspective of Hall conductivities

We start by reviewing the edge perspective and the bulk perspective of the charge Hall and the thermal Hall conductivity, which are expected to produce equivalent results [72]. First, the edge perspective states that the Hall currents are carried by chiral edge modes. More precisely, for charge Hall conductivity σx​y\sigma_{xy}, each chiral edge mode is expected to contribute one quantum e2/he^{2}/h, whereas for thermal Hall conductivity the counting is given by the chiral central charge c−c_{-}:

κx​yT=c−​π​kB26​ℏ.\frac{\kappa_{xy}}{T}=c_{-}\frac{\pi k_{B}^{2}}{6\hbar}\,. (16)

Second, the bulk perspective states that the thermal Hall current exists in the bulk, which can be computed using the bulk wavefunction or equivalently the Kubo formula. At first glance, the equivalence between the bulk and the edge perspective is not obvious, as they predict different microscopic current density profiles in the system.

We try to reconcile the difference by first focusing on the charge response of the integer Quantum Hall effect (IQHE). In IQHE, the edge current picture is obtained by applying a different chemical potential μL≠μR\mu_{L}\neq\mu_{R} to the two sides of the system [73]. In the bulk picture, an electric field is directly applied across the whole system, and by solving the Schrodinger equation with a bulk electric field, it is shown that there is Hall current in the bulk. This example demonstrates that the Einstein relation (equivalence between chemical potential and electrical potential) is broken in the presence of time-reversal symmetry breaking. However, the difference of microscopic current profile between these two setups is the curl of the magnetization, which does not contribute to transport [72], and therefore both of them yield the same Hall conductivity σx​y\sigma_{xy}. To summarize, the edge and the bulk perspectives of the charge Hall effect arise from different protocols of driving transport and the breaking of the Einstein relation.

Next we move to thermal Hall transport. In practice, thermal transport is driven by applying a temperature gradient to the system, but as Luttinger pointed out, it can also be achieved by applying gravity to the system [74]. Similar to the discussion in the previous paragraph, we expect the bulk and the edge perspectives correspond to driving the system with a gravitational field and a temperature gradient, respectively. When time-reversal symmetry is broken, these two perspectives will produce different microscopic energy current profiles because of the presence of energy magnetization. However, unlike the charge Hall case where the two perspectives produce the same Hall conductivity, in the thermal transport case the connection between the two perspectives is further complicated by the fact that energy magnetization also contributes to the thermal Hall conductivity[75, 72], which manifests itself as unphysical divergences of Kubo formula computations at low temperatures[10, 76]. This divergence is associated with microscopic circulating currents entering the Kubo formula[10, 76], which needs to be subtracted using the procedure developed in [77]. After this substraction, the bulk result is expected to be equivalent to be edge result, as we will demonstrate later.

IV Thermal Hall effect in the CSL phase

In this section, we address the thermal Hall effect deep inside the CSL phase. The result of the total κx​y\kappa_{xy} contains contributions from both the fermionic spinons and the emergent gauge fields

κx​y=κx​yspinon+κx​ygauge,\kappa_{xy}=\kappa_{xy}^{\text{spinon}}+\kappa_{xy}^{\text{gauge}}\,, (17)

and we separately address them below:

Spinon contribution: We employ the framework introduced in Ref. [77] to calculate κx​y\kappa_{xy} in the CSL phase. Transforming to momentum space, the mean-field Hamiltonian in Eq. (7) can now be formulated as

HMF=t​∑𝒌f𝒌​s†​ℋ​(𝒌)s​s′​f𝒌​s′,H_{\text{MF}}=t\,\sum_{\bm{k}}\,f^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}s}\,\mathcal{H}(\bm{k})^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ss^{\prime}}\,f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bm{k}s^{\prime}}, (18)

where ss and s′s^{\prime} are the sublattice indices. The diagonalization of ℋ⁡(𝒌)\mathcal{H}(\bm{k}) for the [ϕ,π−2​ϕ][\phi,\pi-2\phi] flux configuration results in the dispersions for the six bands shown in Fig. 2c. Denoting the band energies for each band n=1,⋯,6n=1,\cdots,6 by ϵn​𝒌\epsilon_{n\bm{k}} and Berry curvature by Ωn​𝒌\Omega_{n\bm{k}}, the thermal Hall conductivity for the fermionic system with a nonzero chemical potential μ\mu is given by [77]

κx​yspinon=−kB2ℏ​T∫dϵ(ϵ−μ)2σx​y(ϵ)∂f⁡(ϵ,μ,T)∂ϵ\kappa^{\text{spinon}}_{xy}=-\frac{k^{2}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\hbar T}\int d\epsilon\,(\epsilon-\mu)^{2}\sigma_{xy}(\epsilon)\,\frac{\partial f(\epsilon,\mu,T)}{\partial\epsilon} (19)

where f⁡(ϵ,μ,T)f(\epsilon,\mu,T) is the Fermi function and

σx​y(ϵ)=−∫ϵn​𝒌<ϵd2​k(2​π)2Ωn​𝐤\sigma_{xy}(\epsilon)=-\int_{\epsilon_{n\bm{k}}<\epsilon}\frac{d^{2}k}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\Omega_{n\mathbf{k}} (20)

is the ℏ/e2\hbar/e^{2} times zero temperature anomalous Hall coefficient for a system with the chemical potential ϵ\epsilon. By imposing the constraint of single-site spinon occupancy, the chemical potential μ\mu is determined in a manner that ensures the system consistently operates at half-filling. The associated Chern number is

Cn=12​π​∫d2​k​Ωn​𝐤.C_{n}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int d^{2}k\,\,\Omega_{n{\bf k}}. (21)

In the scenario of an isolated band, distinct from all others due to an energy gap, the Chern number is well-defined and takes integer values. As the temperature approaches zero, Eq. (19) converges to the Wiedemann-Franz law and gives

κx​yspinonT=−2×π​kB26​ℏ∑n∈filled​bandsCn,\frac{\kappa^{\text{spinon}}_{xy}}{T}=-2\times\frac{\pi k_{B}^{2}}{6\hbar}\sum_{n\,\in\,{\rm filled~bands}}\hskip-8.5359ptC_{n}, (22)

where a factor of 22 is multiplied to account for the spin degeneracy. This implies that κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T is quantized in integer units of (π​kB2/6​ℏ)(\pi k_{B}^{2}/6\hbar) at absolute zero temperature.

In Fig. 3, we plot the numerically calculated temperature dependence of thermal Hall conductivity within the CSL phase in the mean-field parton approximation. In the CSL phase featuring semion topological order, the thermal Hall conductivity is quantized to 22 in the limit of zero temperature, and it exhibits a rapid increase as the temperature rises. The initial increase with temperature is on account of the peculiar distribution of the Chern numbers of the lowest bands, C={−1,−1,1,−1},C=\{-1,-1,1,-1\}, where the first three bands are occupied. As the temperature is increased, the first unoccupied band with Chern number −1-1 also starts contributing, which increases the thermal Hall conductivity with respect to the zero temperature limit. At temperatures significantly surpassing the maximum energy of the fermion bands, all the bands are nearly uniformly populated, dictated by the Fermi-Dirac distribution function. At high temperatures, we observe κx​y/T∼T−3,\kappa_{xy}/T\sim T^{-3}, similar to that predicted in Ref. [78] for noninteracting fermionic systems with a bounded spectrum; however unlike Ref. [78], we do not find any intermediate temperature regime where κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T decreases exponentially, i.e., e−T/T0.e^{-T/T_{0}}. For other distributions of the Chern numbers, the thermal Hall conductivity could have a monotonously decreasing temperature dependence. Experimentally, a non-monotonic temperature dependence of the thermal Hall response is seen [62, 63, 64]; however, quantization has not yet been observed.

Gauge field contribution: After determining the thermal Hall conductivity within the mean-field theory, we now investigate how it is influenced by the gauge field. We will calculate κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T at zero-temperature by examining the edge theory of the Lagrangian in Eq. (12). In Section V, we will explore the effect of the gauge field on κx​y\kappa_{xy} from the perspective of the bulk theory using 1/Nf1/N_{f} expansion. From the edge perspective, the total thermal Hall conductivity is given by Eq.(16) in terms of the chiral central charge c−c_{-}. For a non-interacting system, c−c_{-} is equal to the Chern number of the system. This is consistent with the fact that κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T calculated from the parton mean-field theory is quantized to 22 in the limit of zero temperature. For the CSL state, spinons are now coupled to the U(1)(1) gauge field. We can derive the edge theory from the Chern-Simons theory in Eq. (15), described by a chiral compactified U(1)(1) boson CFT, also at level −2-2. The chiral central charge for this theory is given by −1-1. Consequently, in the semion topological order phase, quantum gauge fluctuations are anticipated to modify the prefactor from 22 to the precisely quantized value of 11 [27, 17]. In the analysis below, we obtain the complete temperature dependence of κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T taking into account the effect of U⁡(1)U(1) gauge fluctuations.

V Thermal Hall response of the continuum field theory

The arguments based on chiral central charge are adequate for obtaining the quantized value of the low temperature thermal Hall effect. However, the finite temperature behavior is also of interest in many situations including experiments. For this purpose, we present a large-NfN_{f} linear response treatment that allows a systematic accounting of the gauge fluctuation effects and can be used to understand the finite temperature behavior of the thermal Hall response. Another advantage is that this being a continuum field theoretical treatment is typically simpler to implement than, say, a numerical lattice calculation (see e.g. Ref. [79]). In a couple of recent insightful works [27, 17], the thermal Hall response of the SU(2)(2) Dirac Chern-Simons theory was studied. This theory describes the quantum phase transition between the Néel state and another featuring coexisting Néel and semion topological order. Here we are interested in the U(1)(1) case and examine the thermal Hall response of the low-energy continuum field theory governing the CSL phase described by the U(1)(1) Dirac Chern-Simons theory, as outlined in Eq. (12), in the Nf→∞N_{f}\to\infty limit. The result of our computation is summarized in Table. 1.

In the limit |m|/T→∞\absolutevalue{m}/T\to\infty, the exact values of κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T can be determined through a mapping to the CFT on the edge, utilizing the bulk-boundary correspondence discussed in Sec. III

κx​yT=−π​kB26​ℏ​sgn​(𝚔^)​(|𝚔^|−1);|m|T→∞,\displaystyle\frac{\kappa^{\phantom{0}}_{xy}}{T}=-\frac{\pi k_{B}^{2}}{6\hbar}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\hat{\mathtt{k}})\left(|\hat{\mathtt{k}}|-1\right);\qquad\frac{\absolutevalue{m}}{T}\rightarrow\infty, (23)

where 𝚔^\hat{\mathtt{k}} is defined in Eq. (14). In the abelian case, we find that the large-NfN_{f} treatment up to 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) gives the exact low-temperature value of the thermal Hall conductivity, and matches with the behavior obtained from the Maxwell-Chern-Simons effective theory. In contrast, in the diagrammatic expansion of the thermal Hall response in the SU(2)(2) case, nontrivial contributions appear at all orders in 1/Nf.1/N_{f}.

V.1 The U(1)(1) Dirac Chern-Simons theory

V.1.1 The Lagrangian and Feynman rules

The interacting Lagrangian in Eq. (12) is still written

but the summations over fermion flavors span Nf≫1N_{f}\gg 1 values rather than just four, and the original fermion-boson interaction undergoes rescaling by 1/Nf1/\sqrt{N_{f}}. At finite temperature, Lorentz invariance is broken due to the introduction of a fixed length in the temporal direction. Since most calculations in this paper are performed at T≠0T\neq 0, we choose an equivalent form of the Euclidean action, deviating from the conventional relativistically invariant notation in Eq. (24):

In the large-NfN_{f} framework, each fermion loop is now accompanied by an additional factor of NfN_{f} due to the summation over flavors, and simultaneously, each interaction vertex is scaled by a factor of 1/Nf1/\sqrt{N_{f}}. In the large-NfN_{f} limit of fermion flavors, the Chern-Simons level 𝚔\mathtt{k} is assumed to be of the same order as NfN_{f}. Since all loop contributions to the fermion propagator are suppressed by 1/Nf1/N_{f}, we will use the free Matsubara propagator, which is given by

𝒢0​(𝒌,i​ωn)=−1i​ωn+𝝉⋅𝒌+m​τz.\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k},i\omega_{n})=-\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}+\bm{\tau}\cdot\bm{k}+m\tau^{z}}. (26)

where τμ={i​𝟙,𝝉}={i​𝟙,τx,τy}\tau^{\mu}=\{i\mathds{1},\bm{\tau}\}=\{i\mathds{1},\tau^{x},\tau^{y}\}.

k\displaystyle k =ωn2+kx2+ky2.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\omega_{n}^{2}+k_{x}^{2}+k_{y}^{2}}. (28)

V.1.2 Renormalized gauge boson propagator at large NfN_{f}

The one-particle irreducible self-energy of the gauge field consists of a closed fermion loop, which is 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) in this expansion. Summing the full geometric series of these terms yields the renormalized gauge propagator. The diagrammatic expansion is illustrated in Fig. 4b. So, to derive the Nf=∞N_{f}=\infty renormalized gauge propagator, we first obtain the effective action to leading order in NfN_{f} by perturbatively integrating out the fermions. We will interpret Eq. (25) as an effective theory, where the Chern-Simons term is generated by integrating out the heavy fermionic band situated far from the Fermi level with non-zero Chern numbers. To acquire the U(1)(1) Chern-Simons term at level 𝚔\mathtt{k}, it is necessary to have 2​|𝚔|2\lvert\mathtt{k}\rvert flavors of heavy Dirac fermions with mass MM, satisfying sgn⁡(M)=sgn⁡(𝚔){\rm sgn}(M)={\rm sgn}(\mathtt{k}). In our approach, the bare Maxwell kinetic term, originating from heavy fermion integration, scales with the inverse of MM [17]. Throughout this paper, we will allow |m|/T\absolutevalue{m}/T to vary arbitrarily, while assuming |M|≳T\absolutevalue{M}\gtrsim T, so that the behavior of the heavy Dirac fermion is described by the effective Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory. It is important to note that the Maxwell-Chern-Simons term generated by the heavy Dirac fermion contributes in the same order as the polarization bubble of the light Dirac fermion. The one-loop corrected effective Euclidean action of the gauge field, at leading order in 1/Nf1/N_{f}, is given by

where

m~t=𝚔~2​π​ga​Nf.\tilde{m}_{t}=\frac{\tilde{\mathtt{k}}}{2\pi g_{a}N_{f}}. (37)

We use the long wavelength limits (𝒒=0,i​ϵn→0\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n}\to 0) for the couplings ga⁡(b).g_{a(b)}. We do not consider the static limit (i​ϵn=0,𝒒→0i\epsilon_{n}=0,\bm{q}\to 0) for ga⁡(b)g_{a(b)} in our calculations because in this case at low temperatures and 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0, 1/ga∼|𝒒|2,1/g_{a}\sim|\bm{q}|^{2}, (see Appendix B) and consequently, the topological mass of the gauge field acquires the momentum dependence m~t∼|𝒒|2,\tilde{m}_{t}\sim|\bm{q}|^{2}, which is inconsistent with the physical expectation of a finite boson mass in the topological phase.

It is easily checked that m~t\tilde{m}_{t} interpolates between mt∼6​𝚔^​|m|/Nfm_{t}\sim 6\hat{\mathtt{k}}|m|/N_{f} at low temperatures (T/|m|≪1T/|m|\ll 1) to 6​𝚔​|M|/Nf6\mathtt{k}|M|/N_{f} at high temperatures |m|≪T≲|M|.|m|\ll T\lesssim|M|.

V.1.3 Heat-current operator and thermal Hall conductivity

To compute the thermal Hall conductivity, we require two operators [77]: the heat current, given by

𝑱Q​(𝒓)≡𝑱E​(𝒓)−μ​𝑱N​(𝒓),\bm{J}^{Q}(\bm{r})\equiv\bm{J}^{E}(\bm{r})-\mu\,\bm{J}^{N}(\bm{r}), (38)

and the heat density

K⁡(𝒓)≡h⁡(𝒓)−μ​n​(𝒓),K(\bm{r})\equiv h(\bm{r})-\mu\,n(\bm{r}), (39)

where μ,𝑱E​(𝒓),𝑱N​(𝒓),h⁡(𝒓)\mu,\bm{J}^{E}(\bm{r}),\bm{J}^{N}(\bm{r}),h(\bm{r}) and n⁡(𝒓)n(\bm{r}) are chemical potential, energy current, particle current, local energy density, and local number density operators, respectively. Therefore, at μ=0\mu=0, it is sufficient to compute the energy current and energy density operators, which can be derived from the stress-energy tensor.

The gauge invariant stress-energy tensor of the theory (24) in Minkwoski signature is given by [17]

Tνμ=\displaystyle T^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu}={} i2​[ψ¯l​γμ​(∂νψl)−(∂νψ¯l)​γμ​ψl]\displaystyle\frac{i}{2}\left[\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\gamma^{\mu}\left(\partial_{\nu}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\right)-\left(\partial_{\nu}\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\right)\gamma^{\mu}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\right]
+1Nf​ψ¯l​γμ​aν​ψl−ηνμ​ℒNf,ψ,a,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\gamma^{\mu}a_{\nu}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}-\eta^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu}\,\mathcal{L}_{N_{f},\psi,a}, (40)

where repeated fermion flavor indices ll are summed over.

Since the stress-energy tensor in Eq. (40) depends on both fermions and gauge fields, we express it as follows:

Tνμ=Tν,fμ+Tν,gμ,\displaystyle T^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu}=T^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu,f}+T^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu,g}, (41)

where the fermionic contribution is given by

Tν,fμ=\displaystyle T^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu,f}={} i2​[ψ¯l​γμ​(∂νψl)−(∂νψ¯l)​γμ​ψl]\displaystyle\frac{i}{2}\left[\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\gamma^{\mu}\left(\partial_{\nu}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\right)-\left(\partial_{\nu}\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\right)\gamma^{\mu}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\right]
−ηνμ[i2ψ¯lγα(∂αψl)−i2(∂αψ¯l)γαψl\displaystyle-\eta^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu}\,\bigg[\frac{i}{2}\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\gamma^{\alpha}\left(\partial_{\alpha}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\right)-\frac{i}{2}\left(\partial_{\alpha}\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\right)\gamma^{\alpha}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}
−mψ¯lψl],\displaystyle-m\,\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\bigg], (42)

and the gauge bosonic contribution is

Tν,gμ\displaystyle T^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu,g} =1Nf​ψ¯l​(γμ​aν−ηνμ​γα​aα)​ψl\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}\left(\gamma^{\mu}a_{\nu}-\eta^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu}\gamma^{\alpha}a_{\alpha}\right)\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}
=1Nf​ψl†​(γ0​γμ​aν−ηνμ​γ0​γα​aα)​ψl.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\psi^{\dagger}_{l}\left(\gamma^{0}\gamma^{\mu}a_{\nu}-\eta^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu}\gamma^{0}\gamma^{\alpha}a_{\alpha}\right)\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}. (43)

Taking the space-time Fourier transform of Tν,fμT^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu,f} in Eq. (42) yields

Tν,fμ​(q)=\displaystyle T^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu,f}(q)={} ∫d3​k(2​π)3{ψ¯l(k)[γμ(k+q2)ν]ψl(k+q)\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,\bigg\{\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}(k)\left[\gamma^{\mu}\left(k+\frac{q}{2}\right)_{\nu}\right]\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}(k+q)
−ηνμψ¯l(k)[γα(k+q2)α−m]ψl(k+q)}.\displaystyle-\eta^{\mu}_{\phantom{\mu}\nu}\,\bar{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}(k)\left[\gamma^{\alpha}\left(k+\frac{q}{2}\right)_{\alpha}-m\right]\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}(k+q)\bigg\}. (44)

Switching to the Matsubara frequency domain from Eq. (44), we obtain the fermionic part of the energy-current

Tfi​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=\displaystyle T^{i0}_{f}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})={} −T∑i​ωn∫d2​𝒌(2​π)2(iωn+i​ϵn2)\displaystyle-T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\left(i\omega_{n}+\frac{i\epsilon_{n}}{2}\right)
×ψl†​(𝒌,i​ωn)​τi​ψl​(𝒌+𝒒,i​ωn+i​ϵn),\displaystyle\times\psi^{\dagger}_{l}(\bm{k},i\omega_{n})\,\tau^{i}\,\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}(\bm{k}+\bm{q},i\omega_{n}+i\epsilon_{n}), (45)

where ωn\omega_{n} and ϵn\epsilon_{n} are fermionic and bosonic Matsubara frequencies, respectively. This defines the fermionic part of the heat/energy-current vertex, illustrated in Fig. 5a,

Γfi​0​(k,k+q)=−(i​ωn+i​ϵn2)​τi,\displaystyle\Gamma^{i0}_{f}(k,k+q)=-\left(i\omega_{n}+\frac{i\epsilon_{n}}{2}\right)\tau^{i}, (46)

and we define the gauge bosonic part of the heat/energy-current vertex from Eq. (43), as illustrated in Fig. 5b, as follows:

Γgi​0;α=−1Nf​i​τi​δ0​α.\displaystyle\Gamma^{i0;\alpha}_{g}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}i\tau^{i}\delta^{0\alpha}. (47)

From Eq. (44), we derive the fermionic part of the energy-density as follows:

Tf00​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=\displaystyle T^{00}_{f}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})={} T∑i​ωn∫d2​𝒌(2​π)2ψl†(𝒌,iωn)[𝝉⋅(𝒌+𝒒2)\displaystyle T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\psi^{\dagger}_{l}(\bm{k},i\omega_{n})\bigg[\bm{\tau}\cdot\left(\bm{k}+\frac{\bm{q}}{2}\right)
+mτz]ψl(𝒌+𝒒,iωn+iϵn).\displaystyle+m\tau^{z}\bigg]\psi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l}(\bm{k}+\bm{q},i\omega_{n}+i\epsilon_{n}). (48)

Similarly, the fermionic part of the energy-density vertex is defined, as shown in Fig. 5c, as follows;

Γf00​(k,k+q)=𝝉⋅(𝒌+𝒒2)+m​τz,\displaystyle\Gamma^{00}_{f}(k,k+q)=\bm{\tau}\cdot\left(\bm{k}+\frac{\bm{q}}{2}\right)+m\,\tau^{z}, (49)

and the gauge bosonic part is defined, as depicted in Fig. 5d, as follows:

Γg00;α=1Nf​(−τ0​δ0​α+τα).\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;\alpha}_{g}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\left(-\tau^{0}\delta^{0\alpha}+\tau^{\alpha}\right). (50)

We are ultimately concerned with the stress tensor-stress tensor correlation functions, which are defined as

Πμ​ν;ρ​λ​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=−TV​⟨Tμ​ν​(𝒒,i​ϵn)​Tρ​λ​(−𝒒,−i​ϵn)⟩.\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu\nu;\rho\lambda}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})=-\frac{T}{V}\left\langle T^{\mu\nu}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})\,T^{\rho\lambda}(-\bm{q},-i\epsilon_{n})\right\rangle. (51)

Given our focus on the thermal Hall effect, we limit our analysis to the energy-density and energy-current sectors by setting ν=λ=0\nu=\lambda=0 in Eq. (51). Subsequently, we aim to isolate the component that is antisymmetric in μ\mu and ρ\rho which should give the thermal Hall effect, achieved as follows:

ΠASμ​0;ρ​0=12​(Πμ​0;ρ​0−Πρ​0;μ​0).\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{\text{AS}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}-\Pi^{\rho 0;\mu 0}\right). (52)

As discussed in the Sec. IV, the thermal Hall coefficient is composed of two elements: the standard linear response contribution κx​yKubo\kappa^{\text{Kubo}}_{xy} and the contribution arising from the energy magnetization MQM_{Q} [77]:

κx​y=κx​yKubo+2​MQT.\displaystyle\kappa^{\phantom{0}}_{xy}=\kappa^{\text{Kubo}}_{xy}+\frac{2M_{Q}}{T}. (53)

The value of κx​yKubo\kappa^{\text{Kubo}}_{xy} is derived through the conventional Kubo formula and is determined by the real-frequency retarded heat current-current correlation function ΠAS,Rx​0;y​0\Pi^{x0;y0}_{\text{AS},R}, which is related to the imaginary-time correlation function as follows:

κKubox​y\displaystyle\kappa_{\text{Kubo}}^{xy} =1T​limϵ→0iϵ​ΠAS,Rx​0;y​0​(ϵ+i​0+)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\,\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\,\frac{i}{\epsilon}\,\Pi^{x0;y0}_{\text{AS},R}(\epsilon+i0^{+})
=1T​limϵ→0iϵ​ΠASx​0;y​0​(−i​ϵn→ϵ+i​0+).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\,\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\,\frac{i}{\epsilon}\,\Pi^{x0;y0}_{\text{AS}}(-i\epsilon_{n}\to\epsilon+i0^{+}). (54)

The determination of the energy magnetization proceeds as follows [77]:

2​MQ−T​∂MQ∂T=M~Q,\displaystyle 2M_{Q}^{\phantom{\dagger}}-T\frac{\partial M_{\mathrm{Q}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}}{\partial T}=\tilde{M}_{Q}, (55a)
M~Q=12​i​(∂qxΠAS00;y​0−∂qyΠAS00;x​0)|𝒒→0.\displaystyle\tilde{M}_{Q}=\frac{1}{2i}\left(\partial_{q_{x}}\Pi^{00;y0}_{\text{AS}}-\partial_{q_{y}}\Pi^{00;x0}_{\text{AS}}\right)\bigg|_{\bm{q}\rightarrow 0}. (55b)

V.2 Transport contribution to κx​y\kappa^{\phantom{0}}_{xy} at 𝒪⁡(Nf)\mathcal{O}(N_{f}): the free Dirac fermion

At leading order for large NfN_{f}, we disregard gauge fluctuations, and the thermal Hall conductivity is mainly influenced by a single one-loop free Dirac fermion bubble at Nf=∞N_{f}=\infty, as depicted in the diagram shown in Figs. 6a and 6b, where the contribution is of 𝒪⁡(Nf)\mathcal{O}(N_{f}).

The thermal Hall conductivity of the free Dirac fermion comprises two contributions: one originates from the light Dirac fermion with mass m,m, and the other arises from the heavy fermion that generates the Chern-Simons term in Eq. (24). Upon combining the contributions of the light and heavy Dirac fermions, the resulting thermal Hall conductivity is given by [17]

κx​y(0)=Nf​κx​yD​(m)+2​|𝚔|​κx​yD​(M),\kappa^{(0)}_{xy}=N_{f}\,\kappa^{D}_{xy}(m)+2\lvert\mathtt{k}\rvert\,\kappa^{D}_{xy}(M), (56)

where 2​|𝚔|=2​Nf2|\mathtt{k}|=2N_{f} is the number of heavy fermion bands, and κx​yD\kappa^{D}_{xy} is the thermal Hall conductivity of a single free Dirac fermion given by [17]

κx​yD​(m)=\displaystyle\kappa^{D}_{xy}(m)={} −π​sgn​(m)12T−m2​π[2Li2(−e−|m|/T)|m|/T\displaystyle-\frac{\pi\,\text{sgn}(m)}{12}\,T-\frac{m}{2\pi}\bigg[\frac{2\text{Li}_{2}\left(-e^{-\lvert m\rvert/T}\right)}{\lvert m\rvert/T}
−ln(e−|m|/T+1)].\displaystyle-\ln\left(e^{-\lvert m\rvert/T}+1\right)\bigg]. (57)

In the limit |m|/T→∞\absolutevalue{m}/T\to\infty and |M|/T→∞\absolutevalue{M}/T\to\infty, Eq. (56) simplifies to

κx​y(0)T=−π6​sgn​(𝚔^)​|𝚔^|,\displaystyle\frac{\kappa^{(0)}_{xy}}{T}=-\frac{\pi}{6}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\hat{\mathtt{k}})\,|\hat{\mathtt{k}}|, (58)

which is exactly the first term in Eq. (23).

Fig. 7 illustrates a plot of Eq. (57) for the case of Nf=|𝚔|=4N_{f}=\lvert\mathtt{k}\rvert=4. In the topological phase, the thermal Hall conductivity is precisely quantized to 22 in the zero-temperature limit, consistent with mean-field theory. However, it exhibits a rapid increase with temperature, followed by a gradual decrease after reaching a maximum in the finite-temperature regime. Therefore, the continuum field theory yields a temperature-dependent κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T that exhibits qualitative agreement with the corresponding outcomes obtained from the lattice model as shown in Fig. 3. The unbounded excitation spectrum of the continuum theory results in a different asymptotic behavior compared to the κx​y(0)/T∼T−3\kappa_{xy}^{(0)}/T\sim T^{-3} law we obtained for free fermions with bounded spectra. Here, using Eq. 56 and Eq. (57) we obtain the asymptote

κx​y(0)T\displaystyle\frac{\kappa_{xy}^{(0)}}{T} ∼−Nf​ln⁡22​π​(T/|M|)​(|m||M|​sgn​(m)+2​ sgn​(M)).\displaystyle\sim-\frac{N_{f}\ln 2}{2\pi(T/|M|)}\left(\frac{|m|}{|M|}\text{sgn}(m)+2\text{ sgn}(M)\right). (59)

The difference between the free and bound spectrum asymptotic behavior arises because for the system with the bound spectrum, the specific heat vanishes at high temperatures in accordance with a power-law.

V.3 Transport contribution to κx​y\kappa^{\phantom{0}}_{xy} at 𝒪⁡(Nf)\mathcal{O}(N_{f}): U(1)(1) gauge field fluctuations

Upon investigating the influence of gauge fluctuations within the 1/Nf1/N_{f} expansion, it has been demonstrated in Ref. [17] that certain Feynman graphs, as shown in Figs. 8a and  8b, have the potential to contribute to the thermal Hall conductivity at 𝒪⁡(Nf).\mathcal{O}(N_{f}). However, owing to the non-Abelian nature of the SU(2)(2) gauge theory, it has been shown in the Ref.[17] that both diagrams are proportional to Tr​(σa)\text{Tr}(\sigma^{a}), where σa\sigma^{a} represents Pauli matrices in color space. Consequently, these contributions are identically zero. Therefore, in the limit Nf→∞N_{f}\to\infty, there are no modifications to the thermal Hall conductivity arising from SU(2)(2) gauge-field fluctuations within the SU(2)(2) Dirac Chern-Simons theory [17].

However, since our U(1)(1) gauge field is Abelian, lacking Pauli matrices in color space, it remains uncertain a priori whether there are any corrections to the thermal Hall conductivity due to U(1)(1) gauge-field fluctuations. The determination of potential corrections necessitates the calculation of contributions from both the Kubo formula and the energy magnetization component. In this section, we investigate these graphs and confirm their disappearance, eliminating the need for any corrections. We will first focus on these diagrams in the zero-TT limit (|m|/T→∞\absolutevalue{m}/T\rightarrow\infty), and also assume that the ratio of light fermion and heavy fermion masses, |m|/|M|≪1.|m|/|M|\ll 1.

We write the Matsubara correlators, illustrated in Figs. 8a and  8b, as follows:

Π(1)μ​0;ρ​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=−Nf​ℬ1​(𝒒,i​ϵn)​Dα​β​(𝒒,i​ϵn)​ℬ2​(𝒒,i​ϵn),\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{(1)}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})=-N_{f}\mathcal{B}_{1}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})D_{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})\mathcal{B}_{2}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}), (60)

where

ℬ1​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{1}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})={} −T∑i​ω1​n∫d2​𝒌1(2​π)2Tr[Γfμ​0(k1,k1+q)\displaystyle-T\sum_{i\omega_{1n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}_{1}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\mathrm{Tr}\left[\Gamma^{\mu 0}_{f}(k_{1},k_{1}+q)\right.
𝒢0(𝒌1+𝒒,iω1​n+iϵn)τα𝒢0(𝒌1,iω1​n)],\displaystyle\left.\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{q},i\omega_{1n}+i\epsilon_{n})\,\tau^{\alpha}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}_{1},i\omega_{1n})\right],
ℬ2​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{2}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})={} −T∑i​ω2​n∫d2​𝒌2(2​π)2Tr[Γfρ​0(k2+q,k2)\displaystyle-T\sum_{i\omega_{2n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}_{2}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\mathrm{Tr}\left[\Gamma^{\rho 0}_{f}(k_{2}+q,k_{2})\right.
𝒢0(𝒌2,iω2​n)τβ𝒢0(𝒌2+𝒒,iω2​n+iϵn)].\displaystyle\left.\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}_{2},i\omega_{2n})\,\tau^{\beta}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{q},i\omega_{2n}+i\epsilon_{n})\right]. (61)

Here Dα​β​(𝒒,i​ϵn)D_{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) is the renormalized gauge boson propagator, the complete expressions of which can be found in Eq. (31). Note that the frequency and momentum of the gauge propagator coincide with the external frequency and momentum of the thermal vertices. By employing Eq. (52), we can isolate the part which is antisymmetric in μ​ρ\mu\rho as

ΠAS,(1)μ​0;ρ​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=12​[Π(1)μ​0;ρ​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)−Π(1)ρ​0;μ​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)].\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{\text{AS},(1)}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})=\frac{1}{2}\left[\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{(1)}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})-\Pi^{\rho 0;\mu 0}_{(1)}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})\right]. (62)

We first calculate the transport contribution from the Kubo formula by setting μ=x\mu=x and ρ=y\rho=y in Eq. (62). Additionally, for acquiring the DC response, it is essential to perform an analytical continuation to real frequencies, where i​ϵni\epsilon_{n} transforms into ϵ+i​0+\epsilon+i0^{+}. Subsequently, the limit ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 should be taken after 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0. Consequently, our attention is directed towards the gauge boson propagator Di​j​(𝒒=0,i​ϵn)D_{ij}(\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n}). As 𝒒→0\bm{q}\to 0, Dα​βD_{\alpha\beta} in Eq. (31) experiences an infrared divergence (IR) due to the presence of a 1/𝒒21/\bm{q}^{2} factor in their expressions. Thus, the 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 limit requires careful handling due to these subtleties. This IR divergence can be cured by replacing 𝒒2\bm{q}^{2} with 𝒒2+α2\bm{q}^{2}+\alpha^{2} and then setting α=0\alpha=0 after the integral has been evaluated. After taking the limit 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0 in Eq. (60), we find that the denominator of ΠAS,(1)x​0;y​0\Pi^{x0;y0}_{\text{AS},(1)} becomes even in k1​x,k1​y,k2​xk_{1x},k_{1y},k_{2x} and k2​yk_{2y}, while the numerator consists terms proportional k1​x​k2​yk_{1x}k_{2y} and k1​y​k2​xk_{1y}k_{2x}. Since these terms are odd in k1​xk_{1x}, k1​yk_{1y}, k2​xk_{2x}, and k2​yk_{2y}, they vanish upon integration over momenta and can be safely dropped. Therefore, the diagram in Fig. 8a does not contribute to κx​yKubo\kappa^{\text{Kubo}}_{xy}.

To compute the energy magnetization, we first need to evaluate M~(1)Q\tilde{M}^{Q}_{(1)} in Eq. (55), which is expressed as follows:

M~(1)Q=12​i​(∂qxΠAS,(1)00;y​0−∂qyΠAS,(1)00;x​0)|𝒒→0.\displaystyle\tilde{M}^{Q}_{(1)}=\frac{1}{2i}\left(\partial_{q_{x}}\Pi^{00;y0}_{\text{AS},(1)}-\partial_{q_{y}}\Pi^{00;x0}_{\text{AS},(1)}\right)\bigg|_{\bm{q}\rightarrow 0}. (63)

Before proceeding with the calculation of correlators to evaluate the energy magnetization, it is important to make a few preliminary remarks. First, ΠAS,(1)00;i​0\Pi^{00;i0}_{\text{AS},(1)} is evaluated by letting ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 and then 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0. So, we evaluate the summations over ω1​n\omega_{1n} and ω2​n\omega_{2n} at ϵn=0\epsilon_{n}=0. Moreover, focusing on the limit 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0, we can expand the full integrand in powers of qxq_{x} and qyq_{y}. Subsequently, we retain only the terms of 𝒪⁡(qx)​(𝒪⁡(qy))\mathcal{O}(q_{x})\left(\mathcal{O}(q_{y})\right) in the correlator ΠAS,(1)00;y​0​(ΠAS,(1)00;x​0)\Pi^{00;y0}_{\text{AS},(1)}\left(\Pi^{00;x0}_{\text{AS},(1)}\right) that remain relevant after taking the partial derivative with respect to qx​(qy)q_{x}(q_{y}). This implies that we can directly substitute 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 into the denominator of ΠAS,(1)00;i​0\Pi^{00;i0}_{\text{AS},(1)} which makes the denominator even in ω1​n,k1​x,k1​y,ω2​n,k2​x\omega_{1n},k_{1x},k_{1y},\omega_{2n},k_{2x} and k2​yk_{2y}. Now after performing the partial derivative, we find that the numerator of Eq. (63) consists of terms that are odd in ω1​n,k1​x,k1​y,ω2​n,k2​x\omega_{1n},k_{1x},k_{1y},\omega_{2n},k_{2x} and k2​yk_{2y} and hence, cancel out when integration over all internal momenta and summing over all internal frequencies. Consequently, the diagram illustrating the contribution from magnetization in Fig. 8b also goes to zero.

We also checked similarly using the finite-TT gauge propagator in Eq. (36) that at 𝒪⁡(Nf)\mathcal{O}(N_{f}), there are no modifications to the thermal Hall conductivity arising from U(1)(1) gauge field fluctuations shown in Figs. 8a and  8b.

V.4 Transport contribution to κx​y\kappa^{\phantom{0}}_{xy} at 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1): self-energy and vertex corrections

We will now examine the contributions to κx​y\kappa_{xy} from the theory in Eq. (25) at 𝒪⁡(1),\mathcal{O}(1), which happen to be the leading ones involving the gauge bosons. The Feynman diagrams contributing to this order are shown in Fig. 9. The three corrections are respectively (a) the density of states (DoS), (b) the Maki-Thompson (MT) and (c) the Aslamazov-Larkin (AL) corrections. We discuss each of these below.

V.4.1 The density of states (DoS) and Maki-Thompson (MT) diagrams

In the earlier work related to the SU(2)(2) case [17], it was argued that the DoS and MT [83, 84] diagrams listed in Figs. 9a and 9b, respectively, are not important in the |m|/T→∞\absolutevalue{m}/T\rightarrow\infty limit. The same reasons are applicable here. The DoS diagram is essentially a self-energy correction to the fermion propagator, yielding a fermion mass correction δ​m∝1/Nf\delta m\propto 1/N_{f} in the zero momentum limit since the gauge boson mode is gapped. The DoS diagram can also generate fermion anomalous dimension at higher momentum. However, it turns out that this is exactly cancelled out by contributions from the MT diagram (a vertex correction) in the following manner. Using a gravitational Ward identity [85], it can be shown that the anomalous dimension from the vertex correction cancels that from the self-energy, so the net effect is again a fermion mass renormalization δ​m\delta m consistent with the self-energy calculation. This finite renormalization δ​m\delta m which is an 𝒪⁡(1/Nf)\mathcal{O}(1/N_{f}) correction, can be ignored in the |m|/T→∞\absolutevalue{m}/T\rightarrow\infty limit. Since the corrections are all 𝒪⁡(1/Nf),\mathcal{O}(1/N_{f}), we posit that the DoS and MT corrections are not important even at finite temperatures.

V.4.2 The Aslamazov-Larkin diagram

Thus, the crucial Feynman diagram is the Aslamazov-Larkin (AL) correction [86], shown in Fig. 9c , which consists of two dashed triangle diagrams and two renormalized gauge boson propagators. Based on the gauge invariant stress-energy tensor in Eq. (40), there are four types of diagrams that contribute to the dashed triangle diagram, as shown in Fig. 10.

The first two diagrams are fermion triangles, consisting of three fermion propagators with the stress-energy vertex given in Eqs. (46) and (49), integrated over the fermion momentum and summed over the internal fermionic frequency. These diagrams have the form:

Γ(AL),1μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)=\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}(p,p+q)= −Nf(1Nf)2T∑i​ωn∫d2​𝒌(2​π)2\displaystyle-N_{f}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\right)^{2}\,T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,
×Tr⁡[Γfμ​0​(k,k+q)​𝒢0​(𝒌+𝒒,i​ωn+i​ϵn)​τβ​𝒢0​(𝒌−𝒑,i​ωn−i​Ωn)​τα​𝒢0​(𝒌,i​ωn)],\displaystyle\times\mathrm{Tr}\left[\Gamma^{\mu 0}_{f}(k,k+q)\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}+\bm{q},i\omega_{n}+i\epsilon_{n})\,\tau^{\beta}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}-\bm{p},i\omega_{n}-i\Omega_{n})\,\tau^{\alpha}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k},i\omega_{n})\right], (64)
Γ(AL),2μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)=\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),2}(p,p+q)= −Nf(1Nf)2T∑i​ωn∫d2​𝒌(2​π)2\displaystyle-N_{f}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\right)^{2}\,T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,
×Tr⁡[Γfμ​0​(k,k+q)​𝒢0​(𝒌+𝒒,i​ωn+i​ϵn)​τα​𝒢0​(𝒌+𝒑+𝒒,i​ωn+i​Ωn+i​ϵn)​τβ​𝒢0​(𝒌,i​ϵn)].\displaystyle\times\mathrm{Tr}\left[\Gamma^{\mu 0}_{f}(k,k+q)\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}+\bm{q},i\omega_{n}+i\epsilon_{n})\,\tau^{\alpha}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}+\bm{p}+\bm{q},i\omega_{n}+i\Omega_{n}+i\epsilon_{n})\,\tau^{\beta}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k},i\epsilon_{n})\right]. (65)

The trace integral of Γ(AL),2μ​0;α​β\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),2} shares the same structure as Γ(AL),1μ​0;α​β\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}, but with different momentum dependence (p,α↔p+q,βp,\alpha\leftrightarrow p+q,\beta).

Similarly, the last two diagrams are fermion bubbles, each consisting of two fermion propagators with the stress-energy vertex given in Eqs. (47) and (50). Their expressions can be obtained in the form

Γ(AL),3μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),3}(p,p+q) =−Nf(1Nf)T∑i​ωn∫d2​𝒌(2​π)2Tr[Γgμ​0;β𝒢0(𝒌,iωn)τα𝒢0(𝒌+𝒑,iωn+iΩn)],\displaystyle=-N_{f}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\right)\,T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\mathrm{Tr}\left[\Gamma^{\mu 0;\beta}_{g}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k},i\omega_{n})\,\tau^{\alpha}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}+\bm{p},i\omega_{n}+i\Omega_{n})\right], (66)
Γ(AL),4μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),4}(p,p+q) =−Nf(1Nf)T∑i​ωn∫d2​𝒌(2​π)2Tr[Γgμ​0;α𝒢0(𝒌+𝒑+𝒒,iωn+iΩn+iϵn)τβ𝒢0(𝒌,iϵn)].\displaystyle=-N_{f}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\right)\,T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\mathrm{Tr}\left[\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha}_{g}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k}+\bm{p}+\bm{q},i\omega_{n}+i\Omega_{n}+i\epsilon_{n})\,\tau^{\beta}\,\mathcal{G}_{0}(\bm{k},i\epsilon_{n})\right]. (67)

By combining (64), (65), (66) and (67), we can write the final expression of the dashed triangle diagram as

Γf,(AL)μ​0;α​β=Γ(AL),1μ​0;α​β+Γ(AL),2μ​0;α​β+Γ(AL),3μ​0;α​β+Γ(AL),4μ​0;α​β.\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}=\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}+\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),2}+\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),3}+\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),4}. (68)

After extensive calculations, the details of which can be found in Appendix C, we compute Γ(AL)μ​0;α​β\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})} for a general value of |m|/T\absolutevalue{m}/T. However let us first consider the zero-temperature limit |m|/T→∞\absolutevalue{m}/T\rightarrow\infty, where we obtain (see Appendix C):

Γf,(AL)00;α​β​(p,p+q)\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(p,p+q) =112​π​|m|​Λ00;α​β,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{12\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\Lambda^{00;\alpha\beta}, (69)
Γf,(AL)j​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\displaystyle\Gamma^{j0;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(p,p+q) =i12​π​|m|​Λj​0;α​β.\displaystyle=\frac{i}{12\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\Lambda^{j0;\alpha\beta}. (70)

where

Λμ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)=\displaystyle\Lambda^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}(p,p+q)={} [pμ​(Ωn+ϵn)+Ωn​(p+q)μ−δμ​0​𝒑⋅(𝒑+𝒒)]​δα​β+p⋅(p+q)​(δμ​α​δ0​β+δμ​β​δ0​α)\displaystyle\left[p_{\mu}(\Omega_{n}+\epsilon_{n})+\Omega_{n}(p+q)_{\mu}-\delta_{\mu 0}\bm{p}\cdot(\bm{p}+\bm{q})\right]\delta_{\alpha\beta}+p\cdot(p+q)\left(\delta_{\mu\alpha}\delta_{0\beta}+\delta_{\mu\beta}\delta_{0\alpha}\right)
−(p+q)α​[δβ​μ​Ωn+δβ​0​pμ]−pβ​[δα​μ​(Ωn+ϵn)+δα​0​(p+q)μ]+δμ​0​(p+q)α​pβ.\displaystyle-(p+q)_{\alpha}\left[\delta_{\beta\mu}\Omega_{n}+\delta_{\beta 0}p_{\mu}\right]-p_{\beta}\left[\delta_{\alpha\mu}(\Omega_{n}+\epsilon_{n})+\delta_{\alpha 0}(p+q)_{\mu}\right]+\delta_{\mu 0}(p+q)_{\alpha}p_{\beta}. (71)

This matches precisely with the stress-tensor vertex of the Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory [17]. However, we cannot completely disregard the stress-tensor vertex of the Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory, which arises from the integration process of the heavy Dirac fermion. In this way, we arrive at

Γ(AL)00;α​β​(p,p+q)\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(p,p+q) =g​Λ00;α​β,\displaystyle=g\Lambda^{00;\alpha\beta}, (72)
Γ(AL)j​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\displaystyle\Gamma^{j0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(p,p+q) =i​g​Λj​0;α​β,\displaystyle=ig\Lambda^{j0;\alpha\beta}, (73)

where gg is defined in Eq. (32).

Given the effective vertex function, we proceed to calculate the corresponding AL current-current correlation function, as shown in Fig.  9c, which takes the form

Π(AL)μ​0;ρ​0(𝒒,iϵn)=−T∑i​Ωn∫d2​𝒑(2​π)212Γ(AL)μ​0;α​β(p,p+q)Dβ​λ(p+q)Γ(AL)ρ​0;λ​δ(p+q,p)Dδ​α(p).\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})=-T\sum_{i\Omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\frac{1}{2}\,\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(p,p+q)\,D_{\beta\lambda}(p+q)\,\Gamma^{\rho 0;\lambda\delta}_{(\text{AL})}(p+q,p)\,D_{\delta\alpha}(p). (74)

A symmetry factor of 1/21/2 has been included here. The above expression is valid for arbitrary |m|/T,|m|/T, provided the temperature-dependent expressions for Γ(AL)μ​0;α​β\Gamma_{(\text{AL})}^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta} and Dβ​λD_{\beta\lambda} etc. obtained in Appendix C and Appendix B respectively are used. For simplicity, we first proceed to calculate in the regime |m|/T→∞,|m|/T\rightarrow\infty, where further analytic simplification is possible.

We focus on the antisymmetric component in μ​ρ\mu\rho, which is responsible for the thermal Hall effect:

ΠAS,(AL)μ​0;ρ​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) =12​[Π(AL)μ​0;ρ​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)−Π(AL)ρ​0;μ​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left[\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})-\Pi^{\rho 0;\mu 0}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})\right]

where 𝒩σ​(p,q)\mathcal{N}_{\sigma}(p,q) represent three distinct polynomials in terms of pp and qq:

We note that ΠAS,(AL)μ​0;ρ​0\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})} satisfies the Ward identity, which, however, tells us that

qμ​ΠAS,(AL)μ​0;ρ​0=0,qρ​ΠAS,(AL)μ​0;ρ​0=0.\displaystyle q_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}=0,\;\;q_{\rho}\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}=0. (77)

This suggests that ΠAS,(AL)μ​0;ρ​0\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})} is proportional to ϵμ​ρ​σ​qσ\epsilon^{\mu\rho\sigma}q_{\sigma}. It is convenient to extract the tensor structure in the following way [17]:

ΠAS,(AL)μ​0;ρ​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=mt​ϵμ​ρ​σ​qσ​𝒫​(𝒒,i​ϵn),\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu 0;\rho 0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})=m_{t}\,\epsilon^{\mu\rho\sigma}q_{\sigma}\,\mathcal{P}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}), (78)

and

Here, 𝒫0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) is the zero-temperature contribution, and the finite-temperature part in which we are interested reads

where

ℳ1=\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{1}={} (1+i){(1+i)𝒒2ε𝒑4−𝒑⋅𝒒[(1+i)(𝒑⋅𝒒+𝒒2)+iϵn2](ε𝒑+𝒒2+ϵn2)\displaystyle(1+i)\left\{(1+i)\bm{q}^{2}\varepsilon_{\bm{p}}^{4}-\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}\left[(1+i)(\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}+\bm{q}^{2})+i\epsilon_{n}^{2}\right](\varepsilon_{\bm{p}+\bm{q}}^{2}+\epsilon_{n}^{2})\right.
+(1+i)ε𝒑2[−𝒒2ε𝒑+𝒒2+𝒑⋅𝒒(𝒑⋅𝒒+𝒒2)]−iε𝒑2[3𝒑⋅𝒒+(1+i)𝒒2]ϵn2},\displaystyle{}\left.+(1+i)\varepsilon_{\bm{p}}^{2}\left[-\bm{q}^{2}\varepsilon_{\bm{p}+\bm{q}}^{2}+\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}(\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}+\bm{q}^{2})\right]-i\varepsilon_{\bm{p}}^{2}\left[3\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}+(1+i)\bm{q}^{2}\right]\epsilon_{n}^{2}\right\},
ℳ2=\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{2}={} (1+i){(1+i)𝒒2ε𝒑+𝒒4−(𝒑⋅𝒒+𝒒2)[(1+i)𝒑⋅𝒒−iϵn2](ε𝒑2+ϵn2)\displaystyle(1+i)\left\{(1+i)\bm{q}^{2}\varepsilon_{\bm{p}+\bm{q}}^{4}-(\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}+\bm{q}^{2})\left[(1+i)\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}-i\epsilon_{n}^{2}\right](\varepsilon_{\bm{p}}^{2}+\epsilon_{n}^{2})\right.
+(1+i)ε𝒑+𝒒2[−𝒒2ε𝒑2+𝒑⋅𝒒(𝒑⋅𝒒+𝒒2)]+ε𝒑+𝒒2[3𝒑⋅𝒒+(1+2i)𝒒2]ϵn2}.\displaystyle{}\left.+(1+i)\varepsilon_{\bm{p}+\bm{q}}^{2}\left[-\bm{q}^{2}\varepsilon_{\bm{p}}^{2}+\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}(\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}+\bm{q}^{2})\right]+\varepsilon_{\bm{p}+\bm{q}}^{2}\left[3\bm{p}\cdot\bm{q}+(1+2i)\bm{q}^{2}\right]\epsilon_{n}^{2}\right\}. (81)

It is important to note that 𝒫0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)\mathcal{P}_{0}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) can be obtained from 𝒫β​(𝒒,i​ϵn)\mathcal{P}_{\beta}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) by substituting the Bose-Einstein distribution function nBn_{B} with 1/21/2 in Eq. (80). Hereafter, we have omitted the zero-temperature part.

To compute the thermal Hall conductivity, we begin by examining the Kubo term κx​yKubo\kappa^{\text{Kubo}}_{xy}, which is evaluated in the ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 limit after taking 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0. By examining Eq. (80), we observe that 𝒫β​(𝒒=0,i​ϵn)=0\mathcal{P}_{\beta}(\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n})=0, leading us to conclude that κx​yKubo=0\kappa^{\text{Kubo}}_{xy}=0. A similar conclusion can be reached by directly taking the Kubo or long-wavelength limit 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0 in Eq. (75), where it is evident that ΠAS,(AL)x​0;y​0​(𝒒=0,i​ϵn)=0\Pi^{x0;y0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}(\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n})=0.

The second contribution to the thermal Hall conductivity arises from the energy magnetization, which can be determined by solving the differential equation

2​M(AL)Q−\displaystyle 2M^{Q}_{(\text{AL})}-{} T​∂M(AL)Q∂T=M~(AL)Q;\displaystyle T\frac{\partial M^{\mathrm{Q}}_{(\text{AL})}}{\partial T}=\tilde{M}^{Q}_{(\text{AL})};
M~(AL)Q=\displaystyle\tilde{M}^{Q}_{(\text{AL})}={} 12​i​(∂qxΠAS,(AL)00;y​0−∂qyΠAS,(AL)00;x​0)|𝒒→0\displaystyle\frac{1}{2i}\bigg(\partial_{q_{x}}\Pi^{00;y0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}-\partial_{q_{y}}\Pi^{00;x0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}\bigg)\bigg|_{\bm{q}\rightarrow 0}
=\displaystyle={} imt𝒫β(𝒒→0,ϵn=0),\displaystyle im_{t}\mathcal{P}_{\beta}(\bm{q}\rightarrow 0,\epsilon_{n}=0), (82)

where the correlators on the RHS are evaluated in the static limit, i.e., 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0 after ϵn→0\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0.

In the static limit, we can explicitly perform the momentum integration in Eq. (80) to obtain

𝒫β(𝒒→0,ϵn=0)=\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\beta}(\bm{q}\rightarrow 0,\epsilon_{n}=0)= −i4​π​|mt|​nB​(|mt|)\displaystyle-\frac{i}{4\pi}\,\absolutevalue{m_t}\,n_{B}(\absolutevalue{m_t})
+i4​πTln(1−e−|mt|/T).\displaystyle+\frac{i}{4\pi}\,T\ln\left(1-e^{-\absolutevalue{m_t}/T}\right). (83)

We can now solve the differential equation in Eq. (82) analytically, which yields

M(AL)Q=\displaystyle M^{Q}_{(\text{AL})}={} c1T2+14​π[mtTln(1−e−|mt|/T)\displaystyle c_{1}\,T^{2}+\frac{1}{4\pi}\bigg[m_{t}T\ln\left(1-e^{-\absolutevalue{m_t}/T}\right)
−2T2sgn(mt/T)Li2(e−|mt|/T)],\displaystyle-2\,T^{2}\,\text{sgn}(m_{t}/T)\,\text{Li}_{2}\left(e^{-\absolutevalue{m_t}/T}\right)\bigg], (84)

where c1c_{1} is an arbitrary constant. Thus the physical thermal Hall conductivity is given by

κ(AL)x​yT=2​M(AL)QT2=\displaystyle\frac{\kappa_{(\text{AL})}^{xy}}{T}=\frac{2M^{Q}_{(\text{AL})}}{T^{2}}={} 2c1+12​π[mtTln(1−e−|mt|/T)\displaystyle 2\,c_{1}+\frac{1}{2\pi}\bigg[\frac{m_{t}}{T}\ln\left(1-e^{-\absolutevalue{m_t}/T}\right)
−2sgn(mt/T)Li2(e−|mt|/T)],\displaystyle-2\,\text{sgn}(m_{t}/T)\,\text{Li}_{2}\left(e^{-\absolutevalue{m_t}/T}\right)\bigg], (85)

which reproduces results of κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T of pure Maxwell-Chern-simons theroy in Ref. [17]. The constant c1c_{1} can be determined by inspecting the behavior of κ(AL)x​y/T\kappa_{(\text{AL})}^{xy}/T in the |mt|/T→0\absolutevalue{m_t}/T\rightarrow 0 limit. We observe that κ(AL)x​y/T\kappa_{(\text{AL})}^{xy}/T in Eq. (85) depends solely on the dimensionless variable |mt|/T\absolutevalue{m_t}/T alone. In the high-temperature limit T≫mtT\gg m_{t}, the system is expected to be unaffected by the energy gap (∼mt\sim m_{t}) [17], hence κ(AL)x​y/T\kappa_{(\text{AL})}^{xy}/T should approach zero. Thus, in the T→∞T\rightarrow\infty limit, Eq. (85) simplifies to

2​c1−sgn​(mt)​π6=0,\displaystyle 2\,c_{1}-\text{sgn}(m_{t})\frac{\pi}{6}=0, (86)

which implies that c1=sgn​(mt)​π/12c_{1}=\text{sgn}(m_{t})\,\pi/12. Consequently, when T→0T\rightarrow 0 with mt≠0m_{t}\neq 0, we get

κ(AL)x​yT=π6​sgn​(mt)=π6​sgn​(𝚔^);|mt|T→∞,\displaystyle\frac{\kappa_{(\text{AL})}^{xy}}{T}=\frac{\pi}{6}\,\text{sgn}(m_{t})=\frac{\pi}{6}\,\text{sgn}(\hat{\mathtt{k}});\qquad\frac{\absolutevalue{m_t}}{T}\rightarrow\infty, (87)

which yields the second term in Eq. (23). For temperatures exceeding mt,m_{t}, κ(AL)x​y/T\kappa_{(\text{AL})}^{xy}/T in Eq. 85 has the asymptotic form κ(AL)x​y/T∼sgn​(𝚔^)​T−1​ln⁡(T/|mt|),\kappa_{(\text{AL})}^{xy}/T\sim\text{sgn}(\hat{\mathtt{k}})T^{-1}\ln(T/|m_t|), and the logarithmic factor crucially distinguishes this from the high temperature contribution from the noninteracting fermions. The above analysis does not take into account the temperature dependence of the triangle vertices, nor that of the parameters gg and mtm_{t} in the gauge field propagators. The temperature dependence of the triangle vertices is a feature that does not exist in the pure Maxwell-Chern-Simons counterpart, and reflects the fact that the fermion masses are finite. In the rest of the analysis below, we study the AL corrections up to higher temperatures, T≲|M|T\lesssim|M|, where we expect that a description in terms of the effective Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory for the heavy Dirac fermion is expected to apply.

The AL corrections modify the free fermion results. Since sgn​(𝚔^)=−1\text{sgn}(\hat{\mathtt{k}})=-1 in our case, the AL corrections decrease the quantized low-temperature value of κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T from π/3\pi/3 to π/6.\pi/6. The AL corrections have a monotonous temperature dependence, smoothly decreasing from the quantized value towards zero with increasing temperature, as shown in Fig. 11. Thus the overall temperature dependence of κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T, illustrated in Fig. 12, should show a non-monotonic profile with a somewhat sharper intermediate temperature peak than the free fermion plot of Fig. 7.

Now we analyze the higher temperature behavior. We begin by focusing on the Kubo conductivity. Using the finite-TT gauge field propagators from Eq. 36 and the triangle vertices calculated in the long-wavelength limit (ϵn→0,|𝒒|=0\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0,\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}=0), we find κx​yKubo=0\kappa^{\text{Kubo}}_{xy}=0 (see Appendix C).

Next, we focus on the transport contribution from the energy magnetization. At finite temperatures, the dashed triangle diagrams in the static limit (ϵn=0,|𝒒|→0\epsilon_{n}=0,\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}\rightarrow 0) have the form (see Appendix C):
