After the RHS is evaluated, we now solve the differential equation numerically. Fig. 11 shows the result of the two different approximations (i.e. with or without taking the temperature dependence of the gauge propagators as well as the triangle diagrams associated with massive light Dirac fermion excitations into account). When these temperature dependences are taken into account, the validity of the analysis is now extended to a significantly wider temperature range 0<T/|M|≲1.0<T/|M|\lesssim 1. At even higher temperatures, the excitations of the heavy fermions will result in further finite temperature corrections to the polarizability, triangle diagrams, level and topological mass, similar to those encountered in the vicinity of T/|m|∼1.T/|m|\sim 1. Since |M||M| is the only energy scale in this high temperature regime, we would get κ(AL)x​y/T∼sgn​(M)​T−1​ln⁡(T/|M|),\kappa_{(\text{AL})}^{xy}/T\sim\text{sgn}(M)T^{-1}\ln(T/|M|), for T/|M|≫1.T/|M|\gg 1. This behavior is in agreement with our numerical results in Fig. 11. In Fig. 12 we show the temperature dependence of the total thermal Hall conductivity taking the bare fermion and gauge fluctuations arising from the AL diagrams into account.

We conclude with some comments on the temperature range of validity of the large-NfN_{f} approximation. From Eq. 59, we note that at high temperatures, κx​y/T∼Nf​ln⁡22​π​(T/|M|),\kappa_{xy}/T\sim\frac{N_{f}\ln 2}{2\pi(T/|M|)}, and the 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) AL perturbative corrections become comparable to the bare fermion contribution at a temperature T=Thigh∼|M|​eNf​ln⁡2≫|M|.T=T_{\text{high}}\sim|M|e^{N_{f}\ln 2}\gg|M|.

VI Conclusion and Outlook

In this study, we investigated the thermal Hall conductivity of the Heisenberg model on the kagome lattice in the presence of a scalar spin chirality interaction. We utilized a mean-field formulation with fermionic spinons to derive a low-energy continuum action for the CSL state featuring semionic topological order.

We took two different approaches. First, we introduced the fermionic spinon to do conventional mean-field decoupling of the spin model and subsequently, we numerically calculated the temperature dependence of the thermal Hall conductivity using the formula given in Ref. [77] for the non-interacting system. Second, we discussed how fluctuations in the gauge field could change the quantized values at zero temperature from 22 to exactly 11, based on gravitational anomaly arguments. The limitation of the gravitational anomaly arguments is that it is valid only in the zero temperature limit. In the second approach, we retained only the relevant low-energy spinon degrees of freedom and investigated the linear response thermal Hall conductivity in the resulting continuum Dirac Chern-Simons theory. The results from the two approaches were in quantitative agreement as T→0.T\rightarrow 0.

We also performed a large-NfN_{f} perturbation expansion for systematic accounting of U(1)(1) gauge fluctuation effects in the thermal Hall response, with results summarized in Table. 1. The leading O⁡(Nf)O(N_{f}) contributions to κx​y\kappa_{xy} containing gauge boson propagators were shown to vanish identicaly. The physical origin of such vanishing is qualitatively different from the recently studied SU(2)(2) Dirac Chern-Simons theories in Ref. [17] where the vanishing of such contributions is on account of the tracelessness of the Pauli matrices in SU(2)(2) color space. The leading nontrivial gauge contributions are 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) and are associated with Aslamazov-Larkin (AL) like diagrams containing two gauge propagators and two fermion loops.

We obtained the full temperature dependence of the dashed triangle vertices and the gauge propagators, in a temperature-dependent Maxwell-Chern-Simons approximate form for the gauge field propagator. At low temperatures, the vertices associated with AL fermionic loops become essentially local and the contribution becomes completely equivalent to that obtained from the U(1)(1) Maxwell-Chern-Simons gauge theory [17]. The AL corrections introduce a modification to the free fermion result, specifically by lowering the quantized value of κx​y/T\kappa_{xy}/T at low temperatures. This correction halves the original value from π/3\pi/3 to π/6.\pi/6. However at nonzero temperatures, the temperature dependence of the vertices must be taken into account, for the light Dirac fermions and the gauge bosons have comparable masses. The temperature dependence of the triangle vertices and that of the gauge propagators largely compensate each other, saving the temperature dependence of the topological mass mtm_{t} that now enters the calculations in this regime. We provide explicit expressions for the finite-temperature thermal Hall response by calculating the Aslamazov-Larkin diagram at finite temperature. This computation is performed within the framework of a temperature-dependent Maxwell-Chern-Simons action for the gauge field. At high temperatures, the AL diagrams make a logarithmic correction to the result for noninteracting fermions.

We conclude with some remarks about experimental data on the thermal Hall response of Kagome antiferromagnets. While quantized thermal Hall response has not been reported, a non-monotonic temperature dependence has been observed [62, 63, 64], reminiscent of our parton theory. Recently, thermal transport measurements were performed on disordered herbertsmithite [87]. Although the thermal Hall response was not significant, the field dependence of thermal conductivity was used to extract the defect contribution. The impurity contribution was not consistent with spin-1/21/2 defects. If the CSL ground state has semionic topological order as we argued here, then vacancy defects are likely to localize fractional moments. It would be interesting to see the behaviour of impurity magnetization in real systems as a function of a magnetic field. An important future problem is studying the thermal Hall response in the U(1)(1) spin liquid with vacancies and gauge fluctuations [88].

Appendix B Effective action at Large-NfN_{f}

In this section, we detail the computation of the vacuum polarization tensor of the light Dirac fermion and the renormalized gauge boson propagator in the Coulomb gauge, which are used to calculate the gauge-field correction to the thermal Hall conductivity at both leading and next-to-leading order in the Nf→∞N_{f}\rightarrow\infty limit. We will begin by computing the vacuum polarization tensor at finite temperature and then extend the calculations from Refs. [82, 80, 90] to include massive Dirac fermions with a Chern-Simons term in order to calculate the renormalized gauge boson propagator.

B.1 Computation of Πfμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{f}

To begin, we calculate the fermion polarization function Πfμ​ν​(𝒒,i​ϵn)\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{f}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) as defined in Eq. (30) at zero temperature, which can be expressed as:

Πfμ​ν​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{f}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})={} Nf​T​∑i​ωn∫d2​𝒌(2​π)2​Lμ​ν​(k,q)(ωn2+𝒌2+m2)\displaystyle N_{f}T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{L^{\mu\nu}(k;q)}{\left(\omega_{n}^{2}+\bm{k}^{2}+m^{2}\right)}
×1((ωn+ϵn)2+(𝒌+𝒒)2+m2),\displaystyle\times\frac{1}{\left((\omega_{n}+\epsilon_{n})^{2}+(\bm{k}+\bm{q})^{2}+m^{2}\right)}, (105)

where

Lμ​ν​(k,q)=\displaystyle L^{\mu\nu}(k;q)={} Tr[(iωn−𝝉⋅𝒌−mτz)τμ\displaystyle\Tr\left[\left(i\omega_{n}-\bm{\tau}\cdot\bm{k}-m\tau^{z}\right)\tau^{\mu}\right.
((iωn+iϵn)−𝝉⋅(𝒌+𝒒)−mτz)τν].\displaystyle{}\left.\left((i\omega_{n}+i\epsilon_{n})-\bm{\tau}\cdot(\bm{k}+\bm{q})-m\tau^{z}\right)\tau^{\nu}\right]. (106)

In the zero-temperature limit, we can replace the summation over the Matsubara frequency with an integral:

T∑i​ωn→∫d​ωn2​π.\displaystyle T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\rightarrow\int\frac{d\omega_{n}}{2\pi}. (107)

The integrals can be evaluated using standard Feynman parameter techniques. Using the Feynman parametrization formula

1A​B=∫01d​x​1[x​A+(1−x)​B]2,\frac{1}{A\,B}=\int^{1}_{0}\,dx\,\frac{1}{\left[xA+(1-x)B\right]^{2}}, (108)

Eq. (105) can be expressed as

Πfμ​ν​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=Nf​∫01d​x​T​∑i​ln∫d2​𝒍(2​π)2​Lμ​ν[ln2+𝒍2+Q2]2,\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{f}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})=N_{f}\int^{1}_{0}dx\,T\sum_{il_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{l}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\frac{L^{\mu\nu}}{\left[l_{n}^{2}+\bm{l}^{2}+Q^{2}\right]^{2}}, (109)

where

ln\displaystyle l_{n} =ωn+x​ϵn,\displaystyle=\omega_{n}+x\epsilon_{n},
𝒍\displaystyle\bm{l} =𝒌+x​𝒒,\displaystyle=\bm{k}+x\bm{q},
Q2\displaystyle Q^{2} =x⁡(1−x)​ϵn2+x⁡(1−x)​𝒒2+m2.\displaystyle=x(1-x)\,\epsilon_{n}^{2}+x(1-x)\,\bm{q}^{2}+m^{2}. (110)

The integral can be computed using dimensional regularization. Although closed-form solutions are possible for arbitrary momenta and mass, we expand the result to second order in momenta, yielding:

Πfμ​ν​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=Nf12​π​|m|​(q2​δμ​ν−qμ​qν)+Nf2​π​sgn​(m)2​ϵμ​ν​λ​qλ.\displaystyle\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{f}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})=\frac{N_{f}}{12\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\left(q^{2}\delta^{\mu\nu}-q^{\mu}q^{\nu}\right)+\frac{N_{f}}{2\pi}\frac{\text{sgn}(m)}{2}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda}q_{\lambda}. (111)

Several noteworthy aspects arise from this result. First, the massive light Dirac fermions contribute to gauge field dynamics similar to the Maxwell term fμ​ν2f_{\mu\nu}^{2}, as indicated by the first term in Eq. (111). The second term represents the anticipated Chern-Simons term with level Nf​sgn​(m)/2N_{f}\text{sgn}(m)/2, which renormalizes the bare Chern-Simons term 𝚔\mathtt{k}. A similar calculation can be carried out for the heavy Dirac fermion in the |M|/T→∞\absolutevalue{M}/T\rightarrow\infty limit. This yields a Maxwell kinetic term that scales with the inverse of MM and the bare Chern-Simons term 𝚔\mathtt{k}. In this manner, we obtain the effective Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory with level 𝚔+Nf​sgn​(m)/2.\mathtt{k}+N_{f}\text{sgn}(m)/2.

Using Feynman parameters at finite temperature offers no particular benefit. Instead, we first sum over the fermionic Matsubara frequencies ωn\omega_{n}, followed by integrating over 𝒌\bm{k}. First, we will rewrite the general structure of the fermion polarization tensor at large-NfN_{f} for the light Dirac fermion:

Let us begin by calculating ΠC\Pi_{C}. The angular integrals can be computed analytically using contour integration:

∫02​πd​θ𝒌​1i​A+cos⁡(θ𝒌)=−2​π​iA2+1​sgn​(Re​(A))\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta_{\bm{k}}\frac{1}{iA+\cos{\theta_{\bm{k}}}}=-\frac{2\pi i}{\sqrt{A^{2}+1}}\text{sgn}(\text{Re}(A)) (125)

Although the angular integral can be done analytically, the integral over |𝒌|\absolutevalue{\bm{k}} cannot be expressed in closed form. However, it can be evaluated analytically in the limit where the frequency ϵn\epsilon_{n} and momentum |𝒒|\absolutevalue{\bm{q}} approach zero—or more specifically, when ϵn\epsilon_{n} and |𝒒|\absolutevalue{\bm{q}} are much smaller than the mass scale |m|\absolutevalue{m}. But, the behavior depends on the ratio a=ϵn/|𝒒|a=\epsilon_{n}/\absolutevalue{\bm{q}} [91]. In this discussion, we focus on two specific cases: the static limit a=0a=0 (ϵn=0,|𝒒|→0\epsilon_{n}=0,\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}\rightarrow 0) and the long wavelength limit a=∞a=\infty (ϵn→0,|𝒒|=0\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0,\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}=0). which is constant and vanishes as T→0T\rightarrow 0. It represents the thermal mass, which arises in the longitudinal component without breaking gauge invariance.

Since we have the polarization tensor of the light Dirac fermion for a general |m|/T\absolutevalue{m}/T, we combine Eq. (112) with the effective Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory of the heavy Dirac fermion to obtain the complete polarization tensor, expressed as

and in the static limit (ϵn=0,|𝒒|→0\epsilon_{n}=0,\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}\rightarrow 0), we arrive at the following result:

+Tπ​|𝒒|2​ln((1+e−|m|/T)),\displaystyle{}+\frac{T}{\pi\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}^{2}}\ln{\left(1+e^{-\abs{m}/T} \right)},

where gg is defined in Eq. (32).

B.2 Effective gauge boson propagator Dμ​νD_{\mu\nu}

With the full polarization tensor determined, we proceed to calculate the renormalized gauge boson propagator in the Coulomb gauge. We can decompose the spatial component of the gauge field (aia_{i}) into longitudinal (aLa_{L}) and transverse (aTa_{T}) components [92]:

ai​(𝒒,i​ϵn)=i​qi|𝒒|​aL​(𝒒,i​ϵn)+i​ϵi​j​qi​qj|𝒒|​aT​(𝒒,i​ϵn),\displaystyle a_{i}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})=i\frac{q_{i}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}a_{L}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n})+i\epsilon_{ij}\frac{q_{i}q_{j}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}a_{T}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}), (141)

where aLa_{L} and aTa_{T} are related to the Cartesian components (ax,aya_{x},a_{y}) via

aL​(𝒒,i​ϵn)\displaystyle a_{L}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) =−i​qi|𝒒|​ai​(𝒒,i​ϵn),\displaystyle=-i\frac{q_{i}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}a_{i}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}),
aT​(𝒒,i​ϵn)\displaystyle a_{T}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) =i|𝒒|​(qx​ay−qy​ax).\displaystyle=\frac{i}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\left(q_{x}a_{y}-q_{y}a_{x}\right). (142)

In the Coulomb gauge, where qi​ai=0q_{i}a_{i}=0, the longitudinal component of aia_{i} is zero. Now, we can relate polarization tensor in a0a_{0} , aTa_{T} basis to the Πμ​ν\Pi^{\mu\nu} in the Cartesian basis as follows:

Π0​T​(q)\displaystyle\Pi_{0T}(q) =i​qy|𝒒|​Π0​x​(q)−i​qx|𝒒|​Π0​y​(q),\displaystyle=i\frac{q_{y}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\Pi_{0x}(q)-i\frac{q_{x}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\Pi_{0y}(q),
ΠT​0​(q)\displaystyle\Pi_{T0}(q) =−i​qy|𝒒|​Πx​0​(q)+i​qx|𝒒|​Πy​0​(q),\displaystyle=-i\frac{q_{y}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\Pi_{x0}(q)+i\frac{q_{x}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\Pi_{y0}(q),
ΠT​T​(q)\displaystyle\Pi_{TT}(q) =(δi​j−qi​qj𝒒2)​Πi​j.\displaystyle=\left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{q_{i}q_{j}}{\bm{q}^{2}}\right)\Pi_{ij}. (143)

With the full polarization tensor derived in Subsection B.1 for both zero and finite-TT, we can compute Π0​T\Pi_{0T}, ΠT​0\Pi_{T0}, and ΠT​T\Pi_{TT}.

Using the full polarization tensor both at zero and finite-TT obtained in the Subsection B.1, one can calculate Π0​T\Pi_{0T} , ΠT​0\Pi_{T0} and ΠT​T\Pi_{TT}. We express the full effective action for the gauge field in Eq. (29) using the a0a_{0} , aTa_{T} basis as

(144)

Using the effective action in (144), we can calculate the gauge boson propagators in the a0a_{0} and aTa_{T} basis. However, since all Feynman diagrams involving gauge fields in our main text are expressed in the Cartesian basis, we can rewrite the effective action in the a0a_{0} , axa_{x} and aya_{y} basis as follows [90]:

𝒮⁡[a]=T2​∑i​ϵn∫d2​𝒒(2​π)2​(a0axay)−q​((Π00−i​qy|𝒒|​Π0​Ti​qx|𝒒|​Π0​Ti​qy|𝒒|​ΠT​0qy2|𝒒|2​ΠT​T−qx​qy|𝒒|2​ΠT​T−i​qx|𝒒|​ΠT​0−qx​qy|𝒒|2​ΠT​Tqx2|𝒒|2​ΠT​T)+1ξ​(0000qx2qx​qy0qx​qyqy2))​(a0axay)q,\displaystyle\mathcal{S}[a]=\frac{T}{2}\sum_{i\epsilon_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{q}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\begin{pmatrix}a_{0}&a_{x}&a_{y}\end{pmatrix}_{-q}\begin{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Pi_{00}&-\frac{iq_{y}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\Pi_{0T}&\frac{iq_{x}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\Pi_{0T}\\ \frac{iq_{y}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\Pi_{T0}&\frac{q_{y}^{2}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}^{2}}\Pi_{TT}&-\frac{q_{x}q_{y}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}^{2}}\Pi_{TT}\\ -\frac{iq_{x}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}}\Pi_{T0}&-\frac{q_{x}q_{y}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}^{2}}\Pi_{TT}&\frac{q_{x}^{2}}{\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}^{2}}\Pi_{TT}\end{pmatrix}+\frac{1}{\xi}\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\ 0&q_{x}^{2}&q_{x}q_{y}\\ 0&q_{x}q_{y}&q_{y}^{2}\end{pmatrix}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_{0}\\ a_{x}\\ a_{y}\end{pmatrix}_{q}, (145)

where we add the gauge fixing term 12​ξ​(∇⋅𝒂)2\frac{1}{2\xi}(\gradient\cdot\bm{a})^{2} to the Lagrangian. To derive the gauge boson propagators in (31) and (36), we first invert the 3×33\times 3 matrix in Eq. (145) and subsequently take the limit ξ→0\xi\rightarrow 0.

Appendix C Calculation of the Aslamazov-Larkin diagram

In this Appendix, we calculate the four diagrams, both at zero and finite temperature, that contribute to the dashed triangle diagram, which is subsequently used to determine the Aslamazov-Larkin (AL) correction to the thermal Hall conductivity.

C.1 Dashed triangle diagram in the |m|/T→∞\absolutevalue{m}/T\rightarrow\infty limit

Here, we first demonstrate the zero temperature calculation for Γ(AL),1μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}(p,p+q) in Eq. (64), which can be written as

Γ(AL),1μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)=\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}(p,p+q)={} −Nf(1Nf)2T∑i​ωn∫d2​𝒌(2​π)2\displaystyle-N_{f}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\right)^{2}T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}
×L(AL),1μ​0;α​β​(k,p,q)(ωn2+𝒌2+m2)​((ωn+ϵn)2+(𝒌+𝒒)2+m2)​((ωn−Ωn)2+(𝒌−𝒑)2+m2),\displaystyle{}\times\frac{L^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}(k;p;q)}{\left(\omega_{n}^{2}+\bm{k}^{2}+m^{2}\right)\left((\omega_{n}+\epsilon_{n})^{2}+(\bm{k}+\bm{q})^{2}+m^{2}\right)\left((\omega_{n}-\Omega_{n})^{2}+(\bm{k}-\bm{p})^{2}+m^{2}\right)}, (146)

where

L(AL),1μ​0;α​β​(k,p,q)=\displaystyle L^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}(k;p;q)= Tr[Γfμ​0(k,k+q)((iωn+iϵn)−𝝉⋅(𝒌+𝒒)−mτz)τβ\displaystyle\Tr[\Gamma^{\mu 0}_{f}(k,k+q)\left((i\omega_{n}+i\epsilon_{n})-\bm{\tau}\cdot(\bm{k}+\bm{q})-m\tau^{z}\right)\tau^{\beta}
((iωn−iΩn)−𝝉⋅(𝒌−𝒑)−mτz)τα(iωn−𝝉⋅𝒌−mτz)].\displaystyle\left((i\omega_{n}-i\Omega_{n})-\bm{\tau}\cdot(\bm{k}-\bm{p})-m\tau^{z}\right)\tau^{\alpha}\left(i\omega_{n}-\bm{\tau}\cdot\bm{k}-m\tau^{z}\right)\bigg]. (147)

In the |m|/T→∞\absolutevalue{m}/T\rightarrow\infty limit, we can replace the summation over the Matsubara frequency with an integral. The integrals can be evaluated using standard Feynman parameter techniques. Using the Feynman parametrization formula

1A​B​C=2​∫01d​x​∫01−xd​y​1[A​x+B​y+C⁡(1−x−y)]3,\displaystyle\frac{1}{ABC}=2\int_{0}^{1}dx\int_{0}^{1-x}dy\,\frac{1}{\left[Ax+By+C(1-x-y)\right]^{3}}, (148)

which gives

Γ(AL),1μ​0;α​β(p,p+q)=−∫d​ln2​π∫d2​𝒍(2​π)2L(AL),1μ​0;α​β(ln2+𝒍2+Δ12)3,\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}(p,p+q)=-\int\frac{dl_{n}}{2\pi}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{l}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\frac{L^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),1}}{(l_{n}^{2}+\bm{l}^{2}+\Delta_{1}^{2})^{3}}, (149)

where

ln=\displaystyle l_{n}= ωn+x​ϵn−y​Ωn,\displaystyle\,\omega_{n}+x\epsilon_{n}-y\Omega_{n},
𝒍=\displaystyle\bm{l}= 𝒌+x​𝒒−y​𝒑,\displaystyle\,\bm{k}+x\bm{q}-y\bm{p},
(Δ1)2=\displaystyle\left(\Delta_{1}\right)^{2}= x⁡(1−x)​(ϵn2+𝒒2)+y⁡(1−y)​(Ωn2+𝒑2)\displaystyle\,x(1-x)(\epsilon_{n}^{2}+\bm{q}^{2})+y(1-y)(\Omega_{n}^{2}+\bm{p}^{2})
+2​x​y​ϵn​Ωn+2​x​y​𝒒⋅𝒑+m2.\displaystyle+2xy\,\epsilon_{n}\Omega_{n}+2xy\,\bm{q}\cdot\bm{p}+m^{2}. (150)

The integral is convergent and can be evaluated using dimensional regularization. We expand the result to second order in momenta and, as an example, obtain the following:

Γ(AL),100;0​x​(p,p+q)=124​π​|m|​[3​m​py−px​(ϵn+2​Ωn)].\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL}),1}(p,p+q)=\frac{1}{24\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\left[3mp_{y}-p_{x}(\epsilon_{n}+2\Omega_{n})\right]. (151)

Similarly,

Γ(AL),200;0​x​(p,p+q)=124​π​|m|​[3​m​py−px​(ϵn+2​Ωn)].\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL}),2}(p,p+q)=\frac{1}{24\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\left[3mp_{y}-p_{x}(\epsilon_{n}+2\Omega_{n})\right]. (152)

The computation of the bubble diagrams Γ(AL),3μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),3}(p,p+q) and Γ(AL),4μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),4}(p,p+q) follows a similar procedure to that of the fermionic vacuum polarization bubble. For example,

Γ(AL),300;0​x​(p,p+q)\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL}),3}(p,p+q) =−14​π​|m|​m​py+124​π​|m|​px​Ωn,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4\pi\absolutevalue{m}}mp_{y}+\frac{1}{24\pi\absolutevalue{m}}p_{x}\Omega_{n},
Γ(AL),400;0​x​(p,p+q)\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL}),4}(p,p+q) =0.\displaystyle=0. (153)

By combining all of them, we can write the final expression as

Γ(AL)00;0​x\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL})} =Γ(AL),100;0​x+Γ(AL),200;0​x+Γ(AL),300;0​x+Γ(AL),400;0​x\displaystyle=\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL}),1}+\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL}),2}+\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL}),3}+\Gamma^{00;0x}_{(\text{AL}),4}
=−112​π​|m|​[px​(ϵn+Ωn)].\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{12\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\left[p_{x}(\epsilon_{n}+\Omega_{n})\right]. (154)

Similarly, we can also perform Matsubara summation for Γ(AL),2μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),2}(p,p+q) also. The calculation of the bubble diagrams Γ(AL),3μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),3}(p,p+q) and Γ(AL),4μ​0;α​β​(p,p+q)\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),4}(p,p+q) at finite temperature follows the same procedure as the fermionic vacuum polarization bubble.

At T=0T=0, nF​(E𝒌)=0n_{F}({E_{\bm{k}}})=0, so the result for the zero-temperature case, Γ(AL)μ​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,𝒒,i​ϵn,T=0)\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n};T=0) aligns with that obtained via dimensional regularization, as shown in Eqs. (69) and (70). Therefore at finite TT we can write

Γf,(AL)μ​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,𝒒,i​ϵn,T)=\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n};T)= Γ(AL)μ​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,𝒒,i​ϵn,T=0)\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n};T=0)
+δ​Γf,(AL)μ​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,𝒒,i​ϵn).\displaystyle+\delta\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}). (158)

Before carrying out the integration over 𝒌\bm{k}, a few remarks are necessary. First, after completing the Matsubara summation, integrating over 𝒌\bm{k} becomes challenging with both pp and qq nonzero. However, since our main focus in this section is the transport contribution from the Kubo formula, we first take the long-wavelength limit (ϵn→0,|𝒒|=0\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0,\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}=0) in Eq. (157). As we observed earlier, the fermion polarization tensor can generally be decomposed into two independent transverse projectors. Here, we explore whether a similar decomposition into independent transverse projectors is possible for the triangle diagram.

To proceed, we first take the long-wavelength limit (ϵn→0,|𝒒|=0\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0,\absolutevalue{\bm{q}}=0) in Eq. (69) to extract the zero-TT part which is given by

Γf,(AL)00;α​β\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})} (𝒑,iΩn;𝒒=0,iϵn→0;T=0)\displaystyle(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0;T=0)
=112​π​|m|​(𝒑2−px​Ωn−py​Ωn−px​Ωn−py2+Ωn2px​py−py​Ωnpx​py−px2+Ωn2).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{12\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{p}^{2}&-p_{x}\Omega_{n}&-p_{y}\Omega_{n}\\ -p_{x}\Omega_{n}&-p_{y}^{2}+\Omega_{n}^{2}&p_{x}p_{y}\\ -p_{y}\Omega_{n}&p_{x}p_{y}&-p_{x}^{2}+\Omega_{n}^{2}\end{pmatrix}. (159)

Next, we notice that the dashed triangle diagram satisfies the Ward identities for the gauge boson vertices

pα​Γ(AL)μ​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,𝒒,i​ϵn,T=0)\displaystyle p_{\alpha}\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n};T=0) =0,\displaystyle=0,
(p+q)β​Γ(AL)μ​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,𝒒,i​ϵn,T=0)\displaystyle(p+q)_{\beta}\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n};T=0) =0.\displaystyle=0. (160)

In the q→0q\rightarrow 0 limit, these identities reduce to

pαΓ(AL)μ​0;α​β(𝒑,iΩn;𝒒=0,iϵn→0;T=0)\displaystyle p_{\alpha}\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0;T=0) =0,\displaystyle=0,
pβΓ(AL)μ​0;α​β(𝒑,iΩn;𝒒=0,iϵn→0;T=0)\displaystyle p_{\beta}\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0;T=0) =0.\displaystyle=0. (161)

Following the Ward identities, we can decompose the tensor structure of Γf,(AL)00;α​β(𝒑,iΩn;𝒒=0,iϵn→0;T=0)\Gamma^{00;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0;T=0) into two independent tensors

Γf,(AL)00;α​β(𝒑,iΩn;q→0;T=0)=112​π​|m|(P1α​β−P2α​β),\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};q\rightarrow 0;T=0)=\frac{1}{12\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\left(P_{1}^{\alpha\beta}-P_{2}^{\alpha\beta}\right), (162)

where P1α​βP_{1}^{\alpha\beta} and P2α​βP_{2}^{\alpha\beta} are defined in Eq. (89).

As we are concentrating on the q→0q\rightarrow 0 case, we will omit (𝒒,i​ϵn)(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) from the arguments and use a superscript/subscript LL to denote that we are working in the long-wavelength limit. Together with the stress-tensor vertex from the Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory, which arises from the heavy Dirac fermion, we can now express the general form of Γ(AL),L00;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,T)\Gamma^{00;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),L}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};T) at finite temperature, derived from the Ward identity, as follows:

Γ(AL),L00;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,T)=\displaystyle\Gamma^{00;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),L}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};T)={} A0;1L​P1α​β​(p)+A0;2L​P2α​β​(p)\displaystyle A_{0;1}^{L}P_{1}^{\alpha\beta}(p)+A_{0;2}^{L}P_{2}^{\alpha\beta}(p)
+A0;3L​P3α​β​(p).\displaystyle+A_{0;3}^{L}P_{3}^{\alpha\beta}(p). (163)

We begin by taking the long-wavelength limit Γf,(AL)i​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,𝒒,i​ϵn,T)\Gamma^{i0;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n};T) to extract the zero-temperature contribution, which is given by:

Γf,(AL)x​0;α​β(𝒑,iΩn;𝒒=0,iϵn→0;T=0)\displaystyle\Gamma^{x0;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0;T=0) =i12​π​|m|​𝒳α​β​(p),\displaystyle=\frac{i}{12\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\mathcal{X}^{\alpha\beta}(p),
Γf,(AL)y​0;α​β(𝒑,iΩn;𝒒=0,iϵn→0;T=0)\displaystyle\Gamma^{y0;\alpha\beta}_{f,(\text{AL})}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};\bm{q}=0,i\epsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0;T=0) =i12​π​|m|​𝒴α​β​(p),\displaystyle=\frac{i}{12\pi\absolutevalue{m}}\mathcal{Y}^{\alpha\beta}(p), (164)

where 𝒳α​β\mathcal{X}^{\alpha\beta} and 𝒴α​β\mathcal{Y}^{\alpha\beta} are defined in Eq. (89). Unfortunately, the above tensor structure can not be decomposed into other independent tensors. However, we obtain the general form of Γ(AL),Li​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,T)\Gamma^{i0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),L}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};T) at finite temperature, which can be derived from the Ward identity and is given by:

Γ(AL),Lx​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,T)=\displaystyle\Gamma^{x0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),L}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};T)= Ax;1L​P1α​β​(p)+Ax;2L​P2α​β​(p)\displaystyle A_{x;1}^{L}P_{1}^{\alpha\beta}(p)+A_{x;2}^{L}P_{2}^{\alpha\beta}(p)
+Ax;3L​P3α​β​(p)+BxL​𝒳α​β​(p),\displaystyle+A_{x;3}^{L}P_{3}^{\alpha\beta}(p)+B_{x}^{L}\mathcal{X}^{\alpha\beta}(p),
Γ(AL),Ly​0;α​β​(𝒑,i​Ωn,T)=\displaystyle\Gamma^{y0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL}),L}(\bm{p},i\Omega_{n};T)= Ay;1L​P1α​β​(p)+Ay;2L​P2α​β​(p)\displaystyle A_{y;1}^{L}P_{1}^{\alpha\beta}(p)+A_{y;2}^{L}P_{2}^{\alpha\beta}(p)
+Ay;3L​P3α​β​(p)+ByL​𝒴α​β​(p).\displaystyle+A_{y;3}^{L}P_{3}^{\alpha\beta}(p)+B_{y}^{L}\mathcal{Y}^{\alpha\beta}(p). (165)

Since we have determined the general structure of the dashed triangle diagram at finite-TT, the calculation of the coefficients Aμ;1L,Aμ;2L,Aμ;3LA_{\mu;1}^{L},A_{\mu;2}^{L},A_{\mu;3}^{L}, and BiLB_{i}^{L} at finite-TT will closely follow the procedure for the fermion polarization tensor, as detailed in Appendix B. In this case, too, the behavior depends on the ratio b=Ωn/|𝒑|b=\Omega_{n}/\absolutevalue{\bm{p}}.

We are now ready to compute Π(AL)x​0;y​0​(𝒒,i​ϵn)\Pi^{x0;y0}_{(\text{AL})}(\bm{q},i\epsilon_{n}) in Eq. (74), utilizing the dashed triangle diagram at finite-TT from Eqs. (163) and (164), along with the gauge propagator at finite-TT. To obtain the thermal Hall conductivity, we need to extract the component that is antisymmetric in x​yxy. Additionally, to derive the contribution from the Kubo formula, we must first take the limit 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0. By doing so, we obtain

ΠAS,(AL)x​0;y​0(𝒒→0,iϵn)=0,\displaystyle\Pi^{x0;y0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}(\bm{q}\rightarrow 0,i\epsilon_{n})=0, (166)

and therefore, κx​yKubo=0\kappa^{\text{Kubo}}_{xy}=0.

C.3 Transport contribution from the energy magnetization at finite-TT

The computation of energy magnetization is carried out using a procedure similar to that of Kubo conductivity, with the added consideration of the static limit. To evaluate Γ(AL)μ​0;α​β\Gamma^{\mu 0;\alpha\beta}_{(\text{AL})}, we first perform the Matsubara sum over internal fermionic frequency ωn\omega_{n} at ϵn=0\epsilon_{n}=0, followed by taking the limit as 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0. We now express the general form of the dashed triangle diagram using the projectors, as outlined in Subsection C.2. We calculate the coefficients Aμ;1M,Aμ;2M,Aμ;3MA_{\mu;1}^{M},A_{\mu;2}^{M},A_{\mu;3}^{M}, and BiMB_{i}^{M} in Eq. (88) at finite temperature proceeds similarly to the method used for calculating the fermion polarization tensor, as shown in Appendix B. Here as well, the dependence on the parameter ratio b=Ωn/|𝒑|b=\Omega_{n}/\absolutevalue{\bm{p}} plays a key role. Taking into account that the stress-tensor vertices for the heavy Dirac fermion are derived from the effective Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory, we obtain the result shown in Eq. (90).

With the finite-TT stress-tensor vertices in hand, we now evaluate the right-hand side of the differential equation in Eq. (82). To evaluate, ΠAS,(AL)00;i​0\Pi^{00;i0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}, we sum over Ωn\Omega_{n} at ϵn=0\epsilon_{n}=0. In the 𝒒→0\bm{q}\rightarrow 0 limit, the full integrand can be expanded in powers of qxq_{x} and qyq_{y}. We then retain only the terms of 𝒪⁡(qx)​(𝒪⁡(qy))\mathcal{O}(q_{x})\left(\mathcal{O}(q_{y})\right) in the correlator ΠAS,(AL)00;y​0​(ΠAS,(AL)00;x​0)\Pi^{00;y0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}\left(\Pi^{00;x0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}\right) that are relevant after taking the partial derivative with respect to qx​(qy)q_{x}(q_{y}). Here, we use the gauge propagator in Eq. (36). By doing so, we obtain

M~Q=\displaystyle\tilde{M}_{Q}= 12​i​(∂qxΠAS,(AL)00;y​0−∂qyΠAS,(AL)00;x​0)|𝒒→0\displaystyle\frac{1}{2i}\bigg(\partial_{q_{x}}\Pi^{00;y0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}-\partial_{q_{y}}\Pi^{00;x0}_{\text{AS},(\text{AL})}\bigg)\bigg|_{\bm{q}\rightarrow 0}
=T​∑i​Ωn∫d2​𝒑(2​π)2​m~t2​ga​[gb​𝒑2−2​ga​Ωn2(Ωn2+(gb/ga)​𝒑2+m~t2)2]\displaystyle=T\sum_{i\Omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{\tilde{m}_{t}}{2g_{a}}\left[\frac{g_{b}\bm{p}^{2}-2g_{a}\Omega_{n}^{2}}{\left(\Omega_{n}^{2}+(g_{b}/g_{a})\bm{p}^{2}+\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}\right)^{2}}\right]
=ga​m~t2​gb​[I1−3​I2−m~t2​I3],\displaystyle=\frac{g_{a}\tilde{m}_{t}}{2g_{b}}\left[I_{1}-3I_{2}-\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}I_{3}\right], (167)

where

I1\displaystyle I_{1} =(gbga)​T​∑i​Ωn∫d2​𝒑(2​π)2​1(Ωn2+(gb/ga)​𝒑2+m~t2),\displaystyle=\left(\frac{g_{b}}{g_{a}}\right)T\sum_{i\Omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\left(\Omega_{n}^{2}+(g_{b}/g_{a})\bm{p}^{2}+\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}\right)},
I2\displaystyle I_{2} =(gbga)​T​∑i​Ωn∫d2​𝒑(2​π)2​Ωn2(Ωn2+(gb/ga)​𝒑2+m~t2)2,\displaystyle=\left(\frac{g_{b}}{g_{a}}\right)T\sum_{i\Omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{\Omega_{n}^{2}}{\left(\Omega_{n}^{2}+(g_{b}/g_{a})\bm{p}^{2}+\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}\right)^{2}},
I3\displaystyle I_{3} =(gbga)​T​∑i​Ωn∫d2​𝒑(2​π)2​1(Ωn2+(gb/ga)​𝒑2+m~t2)2.\displaystyle=\left(\frac{g_{b}}{g_{a}}\right)T\sum_{i\Omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\left(\Omega_{n}^{2}+(g_{b}/g_{a})\bm{p}^{2}+\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}\right)^{2}}. (168)

In the above expressions, we use the long wavelength limits for ga⁡(b)g_{a(b)} as explained in Section V.

Let us begin by calculating I1I_{1}, which can be written as

I1=T​∑i​Ωn∫d2​𝒑(2​π)2​1(Ωn2+𝒑2+m~t2),\displaystyle I_{1}=T\sum_{i\Omega_{n}}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\left(\Omega_{n}^{2}+\bm{p}^{2}+\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}\right)}, (169)

where we shift the loop momenta 𝒑→ga/gb​𝒑\bm{p}\rightarrow\sqrt{g_{a}/g_{b}}\,\bm{p}. Using the following summation identity,

∑n=−∞∞1n2+a2=πa​coth⁡(π​a),\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{\pi}{a}\,\coth{(\pi a)}, (170)

Eq. (169) can be written as

=\displaystyle={} 12​∫d2​𝒑(2​π)2​1𝒑2+m~t2​(coth⁡(𝒑2+m~t22​T)−1)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bm{p}^{2}+\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}}}\left(\coth{\left(\frac{\sqrt{\bm{p}^{2}+\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}}}{2T}\right)}-1\right)
+12∫d2​𝒑(2​π)21𝒑2+m~t2\displaystyle{}+\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bm{p}^{2}+\tilde{m}_{t}^{2}}} (171)

The first integral is convergent, and the second, which is divergent, will be evaluated using dimensional regularization. The first integral may be evaluated as follows:

−2Tln⁡([sinh⁡((|m~t|2​T))+])+|m~t|}\displaystyle\left.-2T\ln{\left[\sinh{\left(\frac{\abs{\Tilde{m}_t}}{2 T}\right)} + \right]}+\absolutevalue{\Tilde{m}_t}\right\}
=\displaystyle={} −T2​π​ln⁡([2​sinh⁡((|m~t|2​T))])+|m~t|4​π,\displaystyle-\frac{T}{2\pi}\ln{\left[2\sinh{\left(\frac{\abs{\Tilde{m}_t}}{2 T}\right)} \right]}+\frac{\absolutevalue{\Tilde{m}_t}}{4\pi}, (172)

Using the general result for dimensional regularization,

×Γ⁡(b−a+d2)​Γ​(a+d2)Γ⁡(d2)​Γ​(b),\displaystyle\times\frac{\Gamma{\left(b-\frac{a+d}{2}\right)}\,\Gamma{\left(\frac{a+d}{2}\right)}}{\Gamma{\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)}\,\Gamma{(b)}}, (173)

the second divergent integral in Eq. (171) can be expressed as

Thus, combining Eqs. (172) and (174), we get
